title: Verdicts
text: What IVP diagnoses about the architectural styles and design sets below: where the domain’s change-driver structure mandates a boundary, and where the style invents one instead. Each entry names the thing, states the diagnosis, and links to the page that argues it.

title: Verdicts
text:
1 Architectural styles




Style
Verdict




Hexagonal (ports and adapters)
A chosen encoding, not a domain-mandated decomposition: the ports and adapters are invented wherever they do not coincide with the partition. Its core-is-independent claim is false for the persisted entity.


Onion
A chosen encoding, not a domain-mandated decomposition: the rings are invented wherever they do not coincide with the partition. Its “domain model coupled only to itself” claim is false for the persisted entity.


Clean
A chosen encoding, not a domain-mandated decomposition: the rings are invented wherever they do not coincide with the partition. Its stability ordering is structural self-containment, not real stability.


Layered
A chosen encoding, not a domain-mandated decomposition: the layers are invented wherever they do not coincide with the partition. Its replaceability claim is false for the business rule.


Vertical slice
A chosen encoding over a domain-near axis, not a domain-mandated decomposition: the slices are invented wherever they do not coincide with the partition. Its independence claim is false under a cross-cutting change driver.

title: Unison (M5b)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Algebraic data types with exhaustive pattern matching: Like Haskell, separates cases explicitly
✅ Abilities (algebraic effects): Superior to monads for separating different effect types
✅ Content-addressed functions decouple code from names: Functions identified by hash of their implementation
✅ Structural typing for abilities: Can satisfy ability requirements without explicit declarations
✅ No orphan instances: Type classes (abilities) prevent distant coupling
✅ Distributed computing primitives: Remote ability separates local from distributed concerns

Object Construction:

✅ Immutable data structures by default: No coupling through mutation
✅ Smart constructors via abilities: Construction effects tracked in type system
✅ No global state: Pure functions can’t have hidden dependencies
✅ Content addressing eliminates initialization order: Functions self-contained, no module load order coupling

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Runtime GC decouples memory: No manual memory management
✅ Immutability prevents reference cycles: Simpler GC, fewer leaks
✅ Distributed execution abstracts memory: Remote computation handles serialization automatically
⚠️ GC implementation details not public: Couples performance to runtime implementation

Error Handling:

✅ Abilities make errors explicit: {Exception} Result shows failure in type signature
✅ Algebraic effects compose: Can combine error handling with other effects naturally
✅ Pattern matching on Either/Result: Exhaustiveness checking prevents missed error paths
✅ No unchecked exceptions: All failure modes visible in types

Concurrency:

✅ Distributed computing built-in: Functions can execute remotely without changing logic
✅ Content addressing enables safe deployment: Update function implementation without breaking callers
✅ Abilities separate concurrent operations: Concurrent, Remote abilities explicit in signatures
✅ Deterministic execution: Pure functions compose regardless of execution location

Language-imposed coupling costs:

⚠️ Small ecosystem means limited library choices: Couples solutions to available implementations
⚠️ Codebase manager is novel: Learning curve couples productivity to understanding content addressing
⚠️ Breaking changes during development: Language still evolving, couples code to specific versions

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Content Addressing vs. Naming: Hash-based identity decouples from names but couples to implementation details (changing algorithm changes identity)
Distributed Transparency vs. Network Reality: Remote abstracts distribution but couples logic to serialization constraints
Immutability vs. Performance: Persistent data structures couple performance to structure sharing discipline
Ability Inference vs. Explicitness: Type inference can hide effect requirements, coupling understanding to compiler
Codebase Manager vs. Traditional VCS: Git independence decouples from version control but couples to Unison tooling

Core Coupling Score: 88/100

Verdict: Unison’s content-addressed code and algebraic effects create exceptionally low forced coupling. Content addressing means functions are truly self-contained—no dependency on import paths, build order, or deployment infrastructure. Abilities provide better effect separation than Haskell’s monolithic IO. Main weakness: immature ecosystem and learning curve for content-addressed paradigm.

2 Platform & Ecosystem
Performance Characteristics: 65/100

✅ Own runtime: Predictable performance, its own runtime avoids JVM dependency
✅ Distributed execution: Can distribute computation across machines transparently
⚠️ GC pauses: Inherits JVM GC characteristics
❌ Persistent data structures overhead: Immutability couples performance to structure sharing
⚠️ Network abstraction cost: Remote computation couples performance to serialization/network

Ecosystem & Tooling: 50/100

❌ Very small ecosystem: Limited library availability couples solutions to manual implementation
✅ Codebase Manager is innovative: Content addressing decouples from traditional VCS
✅ Excellent error messages: Compiler feedback decouples debugging from trial-and-error
⚠️ UCM learning curve: Novel workflow couples productivity to understanding new paradigm
✅ Share functionality built-in: Can publish/consume code via Unison Share without separate package manager

Language Evolution: 70/100

✅ Content addressing handles refactoring: Rename functions without breaking dependents (they reference by hash)
✅ Upgrade functions independently: Can use multiple versions of same function (different hashes)
⚠️ Pre-1.0 stability: Breaking changes still occur, couples code to language version
✅ Automatic migration tools: UCM helps update codebases when language changes
⚠️ Small team: Development pace couples to limited resources

Domain Suitability: 80/100

✅ Excellent for distributed systems: Built-in remote execution separates logic from distribution
✅ Strong for backend services: Type safety + distributed primitives
⚠️ Limited frontend use: No browser runtime (yet)
⚠️ Immature for production: Ecosystem couples adoption to risk tolerance
✅ Great for exploratory programming: Content addressing enables fearless refactoring

Learning Curve: 50/100

❌ Novel paradigm: Content addressing + abilities + UCM workflow all new concepts
✅ Good documentation: Unison docs and tour explain concepts well
⚠️ Requires functional thinking: Learning couples to FP background
⚠️ UCM workflow different: Codebase management couples to unlearning Git habits
✅ Interactive REPL: ucm makes exploration easier

Syntax & Ergonomics: 85/100

✅ Clean syntax: Python/Haskell hybrid, minimal noise
✅ Significant whitespace: Indentation-based, reduces boilerplate
✅ Abilities integrate naturally: Effect syntax lightweight
⚠️ UCM commands: Learning curve for codebase operations
✅ Hash-qualified names optional: Can use readable names, hashes only when needed

Testing & Debugging: 70/100

✅ Watch expressions: Can add tests directly in code files
✅ Pure functions easy to test: No hidden state coupling
✅ Property testing support: Can write generative tests
⚠️ Debugging tools immature: Stack traces couple to runtime implementation
⚠️ Distributed debugging hard: Remote computation couples debugging to network

Security: 90/100

✅ Memory safe: GC prevents memory bugs
✅ Type safety: No null, no type confusion
✅ Content addressing: Function identity verified by hash, prevents tampering
✅ Ability system: Can control what effects functions perform
⚠️ Distributed execution risk: Remote computation couples security to network trust

title: PureScript (0.15)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ All Haskell benefits plus algebraic effects: Effect system separates different effect types (unlike Haskell’s monolithic IO)
✅ Row polymorphism for extensible records: Can decouple from exact record shape
✅ Type classes with functional dependencies: More precise abstraction control

Object Construction:

✅ Same as Haskell: ADTs, smart constructors, no global state

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ JavaScript GC decouples memory: Compiles to JS, inherits JS GC
✅ Immutability simplifies: No cyclic mutable references
⚠️ JavaScript GC pauses: Non-deterministic, inherited from JS runtime
✅ No space leaks from laziness: Strict evaluation by default (unlike Haskell)
⚠️ JS interop can create leaks: Foreign JS code may hold references

Error Handling:

✅ Effect system makes errors explicit by type: Effect (console :: CONSOLE, exception :: EXCEPTION) Unit shows exactly what can fail
✅ Explicit exception handling: No hidden runtime exceptions

Concurrency:

✅ Aff monad for async: Separates async coordination from sync logic
✅ Effect tracking prevents coupling: Can’t accidentally do async in sync code

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ JavaScript FFI can bypass type safety: Interop creates coupling holes
❌ Small ecosystem means reinventing wheels: Couples you to specific libraries

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Type Safety vs. JavaScript Interop: FFI boundary loses all guarantees, couples to JS runtime behavior
Effect Granularity vs. Complexity: Fine-grained effect tracking increases cognitive load
Compile Target Constraints: Must fit JavaScript semantics, can’t have true parallelism
Ecosystem Size vs. Quality: Small community means fewer libraries but tighter coupling to available ones

title: F# (9)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Discriminated unions separate cases: Like Haskell ADTs
✅ Type providers decouple data access from code: SQL, JSON, etc. accessed via types generated from schemas
⚠️ OOP interop allows inheritance coupling: Can use C# classes with inheritance, coupling subclasses to base classes

Object Construction:

✅ Immutable records by default: Construction doesn’t couple to mutation
✅ With-copy syntax decouples updates: { person with Age = 30 } doesn’t modify original
⚠️ Can use .NET constructors with side effects: Interop allows coupled construction

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ .NET GC decouples memory: Generational GC handles deallocation
✅ Immutability simplifies GC: Fewer mutable references, cleaner collection
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Non-deterministic pauses, though .NET GC is mature
⚠️ Can use IDisposable from .NET: Manual resource management via use keyword couples cleanup
✅ Garbage collection handles closures: Captured references are traced by the .NET GC, not by reference counting

Error Handling:

✅ Result type separates success/failure: Result<'T, 'Error> makes errors explicit
⚠️ Can throw .NET exceptions: Interop allows unchecked exceptions
✅ Railway-oriented programming pattern: The community embraces this functional error-handling style where success and failure paths are composed like parallel railroad tracks using Result types

Concurrency:

✅ Async workflows decouple async from sync: async { } blocks separate concerns
✅ MailboxProcessor for actors: Message passing decouples concurrent operations
⚠️ .NET threads allow shared mutable state: Interop permits coupling

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ .NET interop is double-edged: Allows violations via C# patterns
❌ Mutable cells exist: Can create ref cells, coupling to mutable state
❌ Nulls from .NET: Nullable references from C# libraries reintroduce null-checking coupling

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Functional Purity vs. .NET Interop: Can’t enforce purity when calling C# code
Type Safety vs. Practical Libraries: .NET libraries use null, exceptions, mutation—F# must accommodate
Railway-Oriented Programming vs. Exceptions: Community promotes Result types but .NET uses exceptions
Immutability by Default vs. Performance: Persistent data structures slower than .NET mutable collections
FP Culture vs. OOP Platform: F# encourages FP but runs on OOP-first platform

Core Coupling Score: 57/100

Verdict: F# provides excellent coupling-reducing features (discriminated unions, Result, async, immutability) but .NET interop creates escape hatches. Pragmatic trade-off: coupling when you want it, C# compatibility when needed. Main weakness: discipline required to avoid .NET coupling traps.

title: C++ (C++23)
text: Analysis against C++23 (ISO/IEC 14882:2024). Older C++ standards have substantially worse coupling properties; C++23 represents the best of what modern C++ offers.

title: C++ (C++23)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Templates enable generic programming: Decouple algorithms from types
✅ RAII separates resource management: Constructor acquires, destructor releases
✅ Concepts (C++20) constrain templates: Clean error messages, explicit constraints decouple interface from implementation
✅ Modules (C++20/23) decouple compilation: import replaces #include, eliminating header coupling
✅ Deducing this (C++23): Eliminates const/non-const overload duplication
⚠️ Multiple inheritance still available: Diamond problem possible (though final specifier helps)
⚠️ Template metaprogramming still complex: Despite concepts, advanced templates couple to expertise

Object Construction:

✅ Constructors separate: Copy, move, default constructors are distinct
✅ Move semantics decouple: Transfer ownership without copying
✅ Designated initializers (C++20): Named initialization decouples from parameter order
❌ Constructors can throw: Exception during construction couples cleanup
⚠️ Two-phase initialization still possible: Though discouraged by modern idioms

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ RAII decouples resource management: Destructors run deterministically, no GC needed
✅ Smart pointers eliminate manual delete: unique_ptr, shared_ptr are idiomatic (manual new/delete is a code smell in modern C++)
✅ std::span (C++20): Non-owning view decouples algorithms from container types
✅ std::mdspan (C++23): Multi-dimensional views with bounds checking
✅ Explicit lifetime management (C++23): std::start_lifetime_as for safe low-level patterns
⚠️ shared_ptr has atomic ref counting cost: And circular references need weak_ptr
⚠️ Raw pointer escape hatches exist: Though idiomatic C++23 uses spans and smart pointers
✅ No GC, deterministic: Full control over allocation timing

Error Handling:

✅ std::expected (C++23): Monadic error handling — composable, type-safe, explicit in signatures
✅ std::optional monadic operations (C++23): and_then, transform, or_else enable composable absence handling
❌ Exceptions still exist and remain unchecked: std::expected is idiomatic and preferred, but exceptions are still in the language and used in the standard library
✅ std::stacktrace (C++23): Provides unwinding visibility, addressing historical debugging pain
✅ std::variant: Type-safe discriminated union for error discrimination

Concurrency:

⚠️ Shared mutable state default: Mutexes required, though lock-free patterns are achievable
✅ std::jthread (C++20): Auto-joining threads with cancellation via std::stop_token
✅ std::latch, std::barrier, std::semaphore (C++20): Higher-level synchronization primitives
✅ std::generator (C++23): Coroutine-based generator decouples producer from consumer
❌ Data races are undefined behavior: No compile-time prevention (unlike Rust)
⚠️ Memory model still complex: Atomic operations require deep understanding

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Macros couple: Preprocessor doesn’t respect scope (though modules reduce header macro issues)
❌ Global state common: Static variables, singletons (not enforced away)
❌ Undefined behavior still exists: Buffer overruns, null derefs possible when using raw pointers/functions
⚠️ Headers still exist for non-module code: #include coupling for code not yet migrated to C++20 modules

Trade-offs (not coupling):

RAII vs. Exceptions: Exception during construction couples cleanup to unwinding, may leak
Zero-Cost Abstractions vs. Compile Time: Templates (and now concepts + modules) couple build speed to abstraction usage
C Compatibility vs. Modern Features: Legacy C patterns can couple to modern C++ code when used
Standard Versions: C++11/14/17/20/23 couple codebases to version choices; modern C++ is largely additive since C++11
Safety vs. Performance: std::span bounds-checking is opt-in; raw pointer escape hatches remain for performance

Core Coupling Score: 54/100 (C++23 — modern idioms with smart pointers, expected, modules, concepts)

Note: C++98/03 would score ~30; C++11/14 would score ~45; C++17 would score ~55. The 67 score reflects C++23 with modern idioms (smart pointers ≥ raw pointers, std::expected ≥ exceptions, modules ≥ headers, concepts ≥ unconstrained templates). Teams stuck on older standards or pre-modern coding styles will experience significantly worse coupling properties.

Verdict: C++23 provides substantially better coupling than its reputation suggests. Modules decouple compilation units. std::expected provides composable error handling. Concepts eliminate template error message hell. std::span/std::mdspan provide safe non-owning views. Smart pointers are idiomatic and eliminate manual new/delete. Main strength: RAII + zero-cost abstractions + deterministic performance. Main weakness: the language retains unsafe escape hatches (raw pointers, macros, exceptions) and new features coexist with old ones, meaning teams must enforce modern idiom discipline. C++23 with Core Guidelines and static analysis is a different language from C++98.

title: Sh (POSIX.1-2024)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 43/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 57/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Sh implements the minimal POSIX shell specification. It has no arrays and no associative arrays. Everything is a string. Functions are minimal, and the original specification had no local variables. Testing uses [ rather than [[. Sh is the most portable but least powerful shell. Global namespace pollution is unavoidable because all variables are global by default.
Platform & Ecosystem: Sh offers maximum portability, guaranteed on all Unix and Linux systems. Dash is commonly used as the /bin/sh implementation. Sh is minimalist by design. Scripts written for sh run everywhere POSIX is supported. Performance is fast due to minimal feature overhead. Sh has no interactive features. The learning curve is gentle because there are few features to learn. It is used for boot scripts and system scripts where portability is critical.

title: C shell (csh 8.2 / tcsh)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 43/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 57/100
Core Coupling Analysis: The C shell, created by Bill Joy in 1978, introduced a built-in expression grammar (borrowed from C) and a strong set of interactive features. But for scripting it scores among the lowest for coupling separation. Everything is words or strings with no type system. All shell variables are global by default, coupling the namespace. The language has no functions; aliases and script recursion are used as workarounds. The parser is ad hoc rather than recursive, so it cannot pipe between control structures (e.g., piping a foreach into grep fails) and produces cryptic errors. The syntax is inconsistent — set, setenv, and alias do the same thing but with different rules, and blocks terminate with endif, endsw, and end needlessly differently. Variable, command, and history substitution create implicit dependencies on execution context. Its strengths are interactive (history !!, aliases, tilde notation, directory stack, job control, path hashing), not separation of concerns.
Platform & Ecosystem: The C shell introduced many interactive innovations later copied by other shells (history, aliases, tilde notation, filename completion, job control). But it has never been popular for scripting, and the POSIX committee favored KornShell for both interactive and scripting use. The original csh has been frozen since 1993 (version 8.2); tcsh is the maintained successor and is what csh usually points to on macOS and many Linux systems. The implementation is criticized for its ad-hoc parser, missing features, and poor error messages (e.g., “0: Event not found.”). It remains on BSD, Linux, and macOS for interactive use and legacy scripts, but Bash and PowerShell are far better choices for scripting.

This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Structural typing decouples from concrete types: Can pass any object with right shape
✅ Union types separate cases: string | number makes alternatives explicit
✅ Generics enable parametric polymorphism: Decouple from concrete types
❌ any escape hatch defeats type checking: Can bypass all compile-time checks, deferring coupling detection to runtime
❌ Type assertions couple to implementation: as Type forces coupling

Object Construction:

✅ Object literals decouple construction: { name: "Alice", age: 30 } without classes
⚠️ Class constructors can have side effects: Nothing prevents coupled initialization
⚠️ Dependency injection requires manual wiring: No built-in mechanism

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ JavaScript GC decouples memory: Generational GC (V8, SpiderMonkey, etc.)
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
⚠️ Closure captures extend lifetimes: Closures hold references, prevent collection
⚠️ Event listeners create memory leaks: Forgotten listeners couple to DOM/event system
⚠️ Circular references with DOM: Can create leaks if not careful with event handlers
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Non-deterministic pauses, though V8 GC is incremental

Error Handling:

❌ Exceptions are unchecked: No throws clause, errors hidden from type system
⚠️ Result types exist but not idiomatic: Libraries like neverthrow exist but uncommon
❌ Promise rejection is unchecked: Async errors not tracked by types

Concurrency:

✅ Async/await separates sync from async: async function makes concurrency explicit
❌ Promises don’t track errors: Promise<T> doesn’t show failure type
⚠️ Event loop is implicit: Single-threaded but callbacks create order coupling

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ JavaScript runtime has no type safety: Types erased at runtime
❌ Module side effects: Imports can execute code, coupling load order
❌ Global namespace pollution: window, global create hidden coupling
❌ Null/undefined everywhere: undefined is default, couples to absence handling

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Type Safety vs. Runtime Reality: Types are documentation only, no runtime enforcement couples safety to discipline
Gradual Typing vs. Type Holes: any escape hatch couples strict code to untyped code
JavaScript Compatibility vs. Type Safety: Must support all JS patterns, even unsafe ones
Type System Complexity vs. JavaScript Simplicity: Advanced types (conditional, mapped) couple to TS-specific knowledge
Build Step vs. Simplicity: Compilation adds complexity, couples deployment to build tools

title: Rust (1.96 / 2024 edition)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Traits decouple without inheritance: Interface + implementation separate
✅ Zero-cost abstractions: Monomorphization prevents abstraction coupling to runtime cost
✅ No null: Option<T> makes absence explicit
✅ Ownership prevents aliasing: Can’t have multiple mutable references, eliminates coupling
✅ Associated types in traits: Decouple trait from concrete types

Object Construction:

✅ Constructors are just functions: new() is convention, not special
✅ Builder pattern zero-cost: Type-state pattern at compile time
✅ No shared mutable state: Construction can’t couple to globals
✅ Drop trait separates cleanup: Destruction logic separate from construction

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Ownership system prevents memory coupling: Compiler prevents use-after-free and double-free at compile time
✅ No GC, no pauses: Deterministic deallocation via RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization, via the Drop trait)
✅ Lifetime tracking decouples: References can’t outlive referents
✅ Zero-cost abstractions for memory: Box, Rc, Arc explicit about allocation strategy
✅ Allocator parameter support: Can decouple allocation strategy from data structures
⚠️ Reference cycles with Rc: Rc<RefCell<T>> cycles require Weak to break
✅ No implicit copies: Move semantics by default prevent accidental copying

Error Handling:

✅ Result<T, E> makes errors explicit: Can’t ignore errors without .unwrap()
✅ ? operator composes: Error handling doesn’t obscure logic
✅ No exceptions: All errors in type system
✅ Panics are rare: Explicit unwrap/expect, or Result

Concurrency:

✅ Ownership prevents data races: Compiler enforces Send/Sync
✅ Async/await with explicit futures: Concurrency in types
✅ Channels separate communication: Message passing decouples concurrent tasks
✅ No shared mutable state without explicit synchronization: Arc/Mutex make coupling visible

Language-imposed coupling costs:

⚠️ Lifetimes can couple: Complex lifetime constraints create dependencies between regions
⚠️ Unsafe blocks bypass memory-safety guarantees: Can violate all guarantees, but explicit
⚠️ Orphan rules couple trait implementations: Can’t impl external trait on external type

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Safety vs. Flexibility: Borrow checker rejects valid programs that don’t fit ownership model
Lifetime Complexity: Complex lifetime bounds couple function signatures to caller context
Async Colored Functions: async fn creates two function worlds (sync/async), couples call sites
Trait Coherence vs. Modularity: Orphan rules prevent implementing external traits on external types
Compile Times vs. Zero-Cost: Monomorphization couples build time to generic instantiation count
Learning Curve vs. Productivity: Steep learning curve couples team productivity to expertise

Verdict: Rust’s design yields exceptionally low language-imposed coupling. The ownership system prevents aliasing and use-after-free at compile time. Result types make errors explicit and composable. Traits decouple interface from implementation without inheritance. Concurrency safety is enforced by the compiler through Send and Sync. title: Java (Java 26)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Interfaces decouple specification from implementation: Can program to interfaces
✅ Generics enable type parameterization: List<T> decouples from concrete types
✅ Sealed classes (Java 17): Controlled inheritance hierarchies — the class author decides which subclasses exist, decoupling from unknown extensions
✅ Records (Java 16): Immutable data carriers with auto-generated equals/hashCode/toString — construction decoupled from mutation
✅ Pattern matching (Java 21): switch expressions + sealed types enable exhaustive, compositional dispatch
❌ No higher-kinded types: Can’t abstract over generic types
⚠️ Type erasure couples generics: Runtime loses type information
⚠️ Inheritance still available: Unchecked class extension possible (unless final or sealed)

Object Construction:

✅ Records are immutable by default: record Point(int x, int y) — no mutation coupling, auto-generated components
✅ Immutable collections (Java 9+): List.of(), Set.of(), Map.of() produce unmodifiable collections
✅ Withers via records: Copy-with-change patterns are built into the language (records + copy constructors)
✅ Dependency injection frameworks: Spring/Guice decouple construction from usage
⚠️ Records eliminate builders for simple cases: Complex multi-step construction may still need builders
⚠️ Constructors couple creation to initialization: Not eliminated, but records and patterns reduce the problem

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ JVM GC decouples memory: Modern GCs (ZGC, Generational ZGC, Shenandoah) provide sub-millisecond pause times
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have dangling pointers
✅ Foreign Function & Memory API (Java 22): Safe memory access without JNI, decoupling native interop from unsafety
✅ AOT object caching with any GC (Java 26): Ahead-of-time object caching reduces startup time and memory pressure regardless of GC choice
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Minimized by modern GCs but not deterministic
❌ Memory leaks from static references: Static collections couple to application lifetime (still possible)

Error Handling:

✅ Checked exceptions separate error paths: throws IOException makes errors explicit
✅ Pattern matching for switch + sealed types (Java 21): Exhaustive error handling — compiler verifies all error cases covered
✅ Primitive types in patterns (preview, Java 26): Extends pattern matching to primitive types, enabling exhaustive switching over numeric domains
❌ Try-catch doesn’t compose: Can’t map/flatMap over exceptions without wrapping
⚠️ RuntimeException bypasses checks: Unchecked exceptions defer error-coupling detection to runtime (sealed hierarchies with pattern matching help)

Concurrency:

✅ Virtual threads (stable, Java 21+): Lightweight threads — each task gets its own thread, eliminating callback coupling
✅ Structured concurrency (preview, Java 21+): StructuredTaskScope — subtask lifetimes scoped to lexical block, preventing thread leaks
✅ Scoped values (preview, Java 21+): Thread-local data with guaranteed cleanup, decoupling context from global state
✅ CompletableFuture: Composable async primitives when needed
⚠️ Shared mutable state still possible: synchronized, volatile, and manual lock patterns remain available

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Null still exists: NullPointerException possible (no non-nullable types in the language)
❌ Static methods couple to global state: Singleton pattern creates hidden dependencies
⚠️ Module system (Java 9+) limits reflection: --illegal-access=deny (Java 17+, default) strictly limits reflective access to exported packages — reflection is no longer a free-for-all
❌ Package-private couples to package structure: Visibility tied to organization

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Checked Exceptions vs. Composition: Explicit errors don’t compose natively (no monadic operations), though sealed types + pattern matching provide exhaustive error handling
Backward Compatibility vs. Modern Features: 30 years of legacy — old codebases can lag behind modern idioms
Null as Default vs. Safety: Everything nullable by default couples all code to defensive checks — records and pattern matching help but don’t solve the root issue
Type Erasure vs. Runtime Types: Generics erased at runtime couples generic code to raw types
Inheritance vs. Composition: Hierarchy coupling possible when teams choose extension over composition

Core Coupling Score: 53/100 (Java 26 with modern idioms — records, sealed types, virtual threads, pattern matching)

Note: Java 8 would score ~45; Java 11 ~52; Java 17 ~60; Java 21 ~65. The 71 score reflects modern Java idioms: records over POJOs, sealed types over open hierarchies, virtual threads over thread pools, pattern matching over instanceof chains.

Verdict: Modern Java (17+) significantly improves coupling over its reputation. Records provide immutability by default. Sealed classes enable controlled hierarchies. Virtual threads transform concurrency from callback soup to structured blocking. Pattern matching with sealed types enables exhaustive error handling. Module system restricts reflection. Main strength: interfaces + records + sealed types + virtual threads create a strong coupling toolkit. Main weakness: null still exists, type erasure persists, and legacy codebases may not adopt modern idioms.

title: Eiffel (ECMA-367 / ISO/IEC 25436:2006)
text: Analysis against the Eiffel language standard (ECMA-367, approved June 2005; ISO/IEC 25436:2006) and EiffelStudio 25.12 (January 2026). Eiffel, created by Bertrand Meyer, is the language that introduced Design by Contract.

title: Eiffel (ECMA-367 / ISO/IEC 25436:2006)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Design by Contract (DBC): require (preconditions), ensure (postconditions), and invariant (class invariants) make an element’s change conditions explicit. This is the coupling-relevant feature: contracts name the requirements an element realizes, so a change in one change driver that forces another element’s contract to change becomes visible coupling across Γ boundaries.
✅ Void safety (attached types): x: attached T vs x: detachable T separates non-null from nullable at compile time (Eiffel 6+). Eliminates the null-checking coupling class at compile time.
✅ Strong static typing: no implicit coercion, no unchecked casts as escape hatches.
✅ No argument overloading: each feature name within a class maps to exactly one feature — “one name, within one class, means one thing.” This eliminates method-resolution ambiguity coupling and is what makes Eiffel’s multiple inheritance safe.
✅ Command-Query Separation: queries (which return information) must not modify the instance — a Meyer design rule that prevents side effects hidden in value retrieval from coupling unrelated elements.
✅ Generics with constraints: LINKED_LIST [G -> COMPARABLE] decouples containers from element types.
⚠️ Multiple inheritance: supported with rename, redefine, and select — powerful feature reuse but creates hierarchy coupling and diamond complexity.

Object Construction:

✅ Creation procedures (create): separate allocation from initialization; create x.make(...).
✅ Invariants validate object state: invariant clauses check well-formedness after every feature call.
⚠️ Creation procedures can have side effects: nothing enforces pure construction.

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Automatic GC: no manual deallocation, no use-after-free, no dangling pointers.
✅ No pointers: memory safety by construction; expanded types give value semantics.
⚠️ GC pauses: non-deterministic, couple timing-sensitive code to runtime.
⚠️ Void references possible (legacy code): without attached-type discipline, dereferencing a void reference raises a Void_call exception at runtime.

Error Handling:

✅ Rescue/retry: structured exception handling where rescue + retry separates error recovery from error detection — failure handling decoupled from the code that triggered it.
✅ Contract-driven exceptions: exceptions arise from precondition/postcondition/invariant violations, making failure points explicit and first-class rather than accidental.
⚠️ Exceptions not used for control flow: Eiffel treats exceptions as contract failures, so error recovery is limited to what the contract model supports.
⚠️ Contracts can be disabled at compile time: EiffelStudio can compile an executable to include or exclude any set of contracts (workbench vs. deployment modes), coupling correctness to build configuration.

Concurrency:

✅ SCOOP (Simple Concurrent Object-Oriented Programming): separates concurrency from logic via processor- and handler-oriented design; decouples “what runs concurrently” from “how it synchronizes” (e.g. multiple threads without explicit mutex management). Available in EiffelStudio, though not yet part of the official language definition.
✅ Agents: wrap operations into objects, closely connected with closures and lambda calculus — decoupling callbacks from the calling code.
⚠️ SCOOP is complex and niche: correct concurrent design requires deep expertise; low adoption.
⚠️ Shared mutable state possible: no compiler-level race detection.

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Once routines create global singleton state: once routines run once (per thread by default, configurable per process or per object) and cache their result — a memoized shared-state coupling across the system.
⚠️ Inheritance still available: class hierarchies couple behavior to the inheritance tree.
⚠️ Small ecosystem: niche community couples solutions to few available libraries.

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Contract vs. Runtime Cost: contract checking adds overhead; disabling it (deployment mode) removes the enforcement.
Inheritance vs. Composition: Eiffel encourages inheritance as its primary reuse mechanism; multiple inheritance couples but enables precise feature reuse via renaming.
SCOOP vs. Pragmatism: the concurrency model is elegant and low-coupling but hard to adopt in practice.
Once Routines vs. Independent Units: memoization decouples repeated computation but couples the element to global shared state that other elements may depend on.
Contract Depth vs. Discipline: DBC only helps if teams actually write contracts; without them Eiffel degenerates to a plain typed OOP language.

Verdict: Eiffel’s Design by Contract is the strongest contract-based coupling tool any mainstream-adjacent OOP language offers: it makes an element’s change drivers explicit and verifiable, so coupling across Γ boundaries is detected at the contract level rather than hidden in implementation. Void safety removes a whole null-checking coupling class that Java and C# still carry. The no-argument-overloading rule and Command-Query Separation eliminate two specific coupling hazards (ambiguous dispatch, hidden side effects). Main strength: DBC + void safety expose and prevent coupling better than almost any OOP language. Main weakness: niche ecosystem, once routines create shared state, and contracts are only as good as the discipline that writes them.

title: Eiffel (ECMA-367 / ISO/IEC 25436:2006)
text:
2 Platform & Ecosystem
Performance Characteristics: 75/100

✅ Compiled to native code: EiffelStudio generates efficient native executables.
⚠️ GC pauses: non-deterministic, though modern GCs keep them short.
⚠️ Contract overhead: runtime checks add cost; disablement improves performance but removes guarantees.
✅ Deterministic when contracts disabled: predictable execution in deployment mode.

Ecosystem & Tooling: 45/100

❌ Small ecosystem: far fewer libraries than JVM/.NET.
✅ EiffelStudio is a complete IDE: integrated compiler, debugger, and contract-aware tooling.
⚠️ Dated tooling: modern build systems and package managers are weak relative to mainstream.
⚠️ Niche community: limited third-party support and resources.
⚠️ Fragmented implementations: EiffelStudio, “The Eiffel Compiler” (tecomp), Gobo Eiffel, SmartEiffel, and LibertyEiffel differ; the GNU implementations track an older language version and do not fully implement the ISO standard.

Language Evolution: 55/100

✅ ISO/ECMA standard: Eiffel is an ISO/IEC standard (ISO/IEC 25436:2006, ECMA-367), giving a stable language core.
⚠️ Slow, conservative evolution: the standard is stable but innovation is glacial.
⚠️ Implementations diverge: EiffelStudio and the GNU-based implementations have drifted on language features.
❌ Niche survival concern: long-term support depends on a small commercial base.

Domain Suitability: 65/100

✅ Excellent for high-integrity and contract-heavy domains: DBC is ideal where correctness is paramount and reliability is the design goal.
✅ Good for teaching design-by-contract: the language enforces the discipline.
⚠️ Poor for mainstream web/systems: GC, niche ecosystem, dated tooling.
⚠️ Little adoption in modern development: hard to hire for.

Learning Curve: 55/100

✅ DBC is a clear mental model: contracts make intent explicit.
⚠️ Multiple inheritance + renaming complexity: advanced Eiffel is hard to master.
⚠️ SCOOP adds a second learning curve: the concurrency model is non-trivial.
⚠️ Fewer modern resources: documentation is dated relative to mainstream languages.

Syntax & Ergonomics: 65/100

✅ Readable, English-like: if x then ... else ... end, require/ensure/invariant read naturally.
✅ Explicit contracts: the syntax makes specification a visible part of every feature.
⚠️ Verbose: end clauses and full declarations add ceremony.
⚠️ Non-standard keywords: keywords (e.g. feature, deferred, attached) are unfamiliar to most programmers.

Testing & Debugging: 70/100

✅ Contracts enable automated testing: preconditions/postconditions/invariants act as built-in test assertions.
✅ EiffelStudio debugger: contract-aware, can inspect invariant violations.
✅ Exception handling tools: rescue/retry makes error paths debuggable.
⚠️ Few third-party test frameworks: the ecosystem is thin.

Security: 85/100

✅ Memory safe: GC, no pointers, no use-after-free, no buffer overflows.
✅ Void safety: prevents null-pointer vulnerabilities by default (with attached types).
✅ Strong typing: no type-confusion bugs.
✅ No argument overloading: unambiguous feature resolution reduces surprising dispatch.
⚠️ Once-routine shared state: can create hidden shared-state vulnerabilities.

title: Turbo Pascal (7.0)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 46/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 54/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Turbo Pascal, developed by Anders Hejlsberg at Borland (1983), is notable for coupling because its units provide a real interface/implementation boundary: interface and implementation keywords control what is visible outside a unit, and uses declares the dependency explicitly. This makes coupling between units explicit and limits it, a strength rare among its 1980s peers. It is strongly and statically typed. Its weaknesses reflect its era. Version 7’s exception handling (try/except/finally) is a 1992 addition and simple — many programs still used manual error codes. Single-inheritance object-oriented programming (added in 5.5) can couple class hierarchies; there are no generics; and memory management is manual. The compiler’s legendary speed (a one-pass compiler) and the integrated IDE made the edit-compile-run cycle extremely fast. Namespaces are limited to units; .TPU object files are compiler-specific and not linkable with other languages.
Platform & Ecosystem: Turbo Pascal had enormous historical influence and reach (over 400,000 copies in two years), and it made Pascal accessible to a generation of programmers. It was discontinued in 1995 in favor of Delphi/Object Pascal, which still supports most of its language. Free Pascal and Virtual Pascal provide compatible implementations, so much Turbo Pascal code can still compile today. Performance is excellent for its era (fast compilation and execution). The ecosystem is legacy DOS/early-Windows. The learning curve is gentle — Pascal’s structured, readable syntax is ideal for teaching. Tooling is historical (the IDE had debugging but no testing framework). It matters today mainly for education and legacy migration, not new development.

text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 85/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 69/100
Core Coupling Analysis: SPARK is a formally verifiable subset of Ada. Flow analysis prevents information coupling by making data dependencies explicit and verifiable. The absence of runtime errors, proven at compile time by the GNATprove tool, decouples program correctness from testing coverage. No aliasing (no pointers) eliminates coupling through shared mutable references. Contracts (preconditions, postconditions, and invariants) are mathematically verified rather than merely asserted. Global variables require explicit data flow contracts stating which globals a subprogram reads and writes. The separation of concerns is not merely encouraged but proven by the toolchain.
Platform & Ecosystem: SPARK targets the highest-assurance systems in aviation, space, and medical devices where software failure costs lives. The learning curve is very steep, requiring both formal methods expertise and Ada knowledge. Tooling is excellent with GNATprove and SPARK Pro. Zero-defect software is achievable with sufficient verification effort. Performance matches Ada since SPARK compiles to the same native code. The ecosystem is a subset of Ada’s. Security is at the maximum possible level: buffer overflows, use-after-free, and other classic vulnerabilities are proven absent. SPARK is used by Airbus, Thales, and Lockheed Martin.

title: Python (3.14)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

❌ Dynamic typing: All coupling at runtime
✅ Duck typing radical: If it quacks, it’s a duck—maximum runtime decoupling
✅ match/case structural pattern matching (3.10+): Exhaustive dispatch on data structures, like Rust/Swift
✅ | union type syntax (3.10+): str | int cleaner than Union[str, int]
⚠️ Type hints (PEP 484) help: Gradual typing, but not enforced by the runtime; mypy/pyright provide enforcement at build time
⚠️ Protocols (PEP 544): Structural typing like Go, but runtime only

Object Construction:

⚠️ __init__ can have side effects: Constructors couple to initialization
✅ Dataclasses decouple: Auto-generated methods; kw_only, slots options improve control
⚠️ Multiple inheritance: Diamond problem; MRO (Method Resolution Order) couples resolution to inheritance order
✅ @override decorator (3.12): Catches broken overrides at check time

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Reference counting + GC: Immediate deallocation for most objects
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
⚠️ Reference cycles need GC: Cycle detector runs periodically
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Cycle collection can pause
❌ __del__ timing non-deterministic: Finalizers unreliable for resource cleanup
✅ Context managers for resources: with statement provides deterministic cleanup
❌ Global references common: Module-level variables extend lifetimes

Error Handling:

❌ Exceptions unchecked: No type tracking in signatures
✅ Exception groups + except* (3.11+): Can handle multiple concurrent exceptions without losing information
❌ Broad exception catching couples: except Exception catches too much
⚠️ Result types possible: Libraries exist but not idiomatic

Concurrency:

✅ Free-threaded Python (3.14, officially supported): GIL removed as opt-in — threads can use multiple cores. Single-threaded performance overhead ~5-10%.
⚠️ GIL still default: Free-threaded mode is opt-in via --disable-gil build or python3.14t
✅ Async/await separates: Explicit async functions
⚠️ Multiprocessing decouples: Separate processes, but manual (less necessary with free-threaded mode)
⚠️ Free-threaded mode is new: Ecosystem still adapting; many C extensions need GIL

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Global mutable state common: Module-level variables couple
❌ Monkey patching couples: Can modify anything at runtime
❌ Import side effects: Module execution couples to import
❌ Mutable default arguments: def f(x=[]) couples calls together
❌ None everywhere: Couples to absence checking

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Dynamic Typing vs. Maintainability: All coupling invisible until runtime, couples correctness to testing — mitigated by mypy/pyright in CI
Free-threaded Mode vs. Ecosystem Readiness: GIL removal is real but opt-in; many libraries haven’t adapted
Monkey Patching: Can modify stdlib/libraries at runtime, couples code to load order
Mutable Default Arguments: def f(x=[]) shares state across calls, couples invocations
Import Side Effects: Modules execute on import, couples import order to behavior
Duck Typing vs. Protocols: No interface enforcement couples to runtime type checking — statically checked by type checkers

Note on concurrency: The coupling analysis gives Python partial credit for free-threaded mode (3.14+, officially supported). The GIL is still the default, but it’s no longer a permanent restriction. Teams deploying free-threaded Python 3.14 can eliminate GIL-based threading coupling entirely. The 55 score reflects this transitional state; free-threaded-by-default Python would score ~65.

Verdict: Python’s duck typing provides maximum runtime flexibility but zero compile-time low coupling by language design. Free-threaded mode (3.14) eliminates the historical GIL concurrency coupling, though it’s still opt-in. Pattern matching (3.10+) and exception groups (3.11+) improve error handling composition. Type checkers (mypy/pyright) provide static coupling detection at build time but not at runtime. Main strength: simplicity, ecosystem, libraries. Main weakness: all coupling invisible until runtime; runtime type safety depends on test coverage.

title: Groovy (5.x)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 53/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 80/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Groovy is a Java-compatible, multi-paradigm language for the JVM that can be both dynamically and statically typed. Its dual typing is the central coupling issue: dynamic typing (the def keyword) defers coupling detection to runtime, while optional static compilation and static type checking (Groovy 2+) provide compile-time detection and near-Java performance. Closures act like method pointers, decoupling callbacks from calling code. Traits (interfaces carrying default implementations and state) support behavior composition without inheritance coupling. The safe-navigation operator ?. reduces null-checking coupling. However, prototype extension via ExpandoMetaClass and Objective-C-style categories enable metaprogramming that can create hidden, action-at-a-distance coupling at runtime. GroovyBeans auto-generate getters/setters, reducing construction boilerplate. Much of Groovy’s power lies in AST transformations (compile-time metaprogramming), which add flexibility without runtime penalty but couple code to compile-time semantics. Groovy’s syntax omitting parentheses and dots enables DSLs that decouple surface syntax from meaning. The JVM ecosystem and tools such as Gradle and Jenkins pipelines make Groovy widely used for scripting and build automation.
Platform & Ecosystem: Groovy has a strong, well-established ecosystem as an Apache top-level project. It is central to Gradle (build automation) and Jenkins Pipeline (CI), and powers Grails web development. Performance is moderate in dynamic mode (JVM, dynamic dispatch) but approaches Java with static compilation. The learning curve is gentle for Java developers, since most valid Java is valid Groovy. The syntax is concise and Java-compatible. Testing is excellent via Spock and JUnit. Security is reasonable, though dynamic typing and metaprogramming (ExpandoMetaClass) can create type-confusion and hidden-coupling risk. The language has no fixed release cadence; Groovy 5.x (2025) improves performance and JDK 17+ support.

title: SQL (ANSI SQL:2023)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 85/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 80/100
Core Coupling Analysis: SQL’s declarative query model separates the specification of what data to retrieve from the procedural how of accessing it. The schema separates data structure from queries that consume it. Views decouple presentation logic from the underlying tables. Stored procedures, however, couple application logic to the database engine. Triggers create implicit coupling by executing side effects automatically in response to data changes. Vendor-specific SQL syntax couples queries to a particular database management system. Normalization decouples data redundancy by structuring tables to eliminate duplication.
Platform & Ecosystem: SQL is the universal standard for data querying and manipulation. Every major database system uses SQL in some form. Fragmentation persists across MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server, though ANSI SQL standards reduce this. Performance is excellent because decades of query optimization research deliver efficient execution plans. The learning curve is gentle for basic queries but steep for query optimization and complex joins. SQL injection remains a major security risk because queries are constructed as strings rather than parameterized by default.

title: Design
text:
Software design is the broad concern of how software is structured. Architecture is a part of design — the decisions that are hard to change — but not all design is architecture.
This section organizes software design into:

Architecture — the part of design concerned with module boundaries and system-level structure.
Languages — the design of, and analysis of, programming languages.
Cohesion — cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule; the (purity, completeness) pair; the knowledge-embodiment theorem.
Coupling — coupling is access to a shared resource; coupling is a consequence of cohesion; the coupling floor.

The five CUPID properties are assessed separately: CUPID tests them against the assessment requirement their author set, and against the standards that define engineering.
The change-management account of module structure that underlies the design analysis is published in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].




References

[1] Y. Loth, “The independent variation principle.” Zenodo, Jun. 2026. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.20794332.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
text: The coupling series supplies what the coupling literature has never had: an ontological account of what coupling is across all its manifestations. Five decades of dimensions, metrics, and measurement frameworks produced no such account. This page collects what the coupling series concludes.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 1 Coupling is access to a shared resource
text:
1 Coupling is access to a shared resource
The central definitional result: two elements are coupled exactly when they access a shared resource.
A resource is anything whose definition, state, or capacity constrains the elements that share it — a module’s interface, a type definition, a database schema, a release pipeline, a team boundary, a deployment unit, a CPU core. A coupling is the ternary relation
(e1,r,e2) (e_1, r, e_2) 
— two entities together with the resource that links them. The resource is the medium of the coupling.
The definition is change-independent: coupling is a standing constraint that holds whether or not any change occurs. Interference and shared fate are couplings that need no change at all.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 2 The recognized dimensions differ only in the resource
text:
2 The recognized dimensions differ only in the resource
Every recognized coupling dimension — structural, temporal, concurrency, semantic, platform — differs only in which resource is shared and how the sharing is enforced. There is no structural difference underneath.
The series provides a taxonomy of resource types organized by seven constraint-kinds (contract, store, medium, budget, authority, location, time) and three coupling modes (definitional, state, capacity). Each coupling dimension maps to its resource, its governing contract, and its enforcement mechanism.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 3 Necessary coupling is to be made manifest, not minimized
text:
3 Necessary coupling is to be made manifest, not minimized
The visibility principle: coupling is not to be minimized but made manifest. Each shared resource is governed by an explicit contract whose violation is immediately detectable.
This reframes the classical imperative. The goal is not to eliminate coupling — coupling is a standing constraint of any system that shares resources — but to make it visible and governed. The directive applies to necessary coupling: the shared-resource edges the system genuinely requires. Accidental coupling is a different target, and it is removed, not merely made visible. The two directives are not in tension because they operate on disjoint edge sets — the visibility principle governs the edges the system needs, while the grouping result below removes the edges above the floor.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 4 Grouping by identical resource-access minimizes accidental coupling
text:
4 Grouping by identical resource-access minimizes accidental coupling
From the coupling definition alone — without change drivers, Γ, or IVP — one result follows: grouping elements by identical resource-access sets
R(e1)=R(e2) R(e_1) = R(e_2) 
minimizes accidental coupling cost.
The series reveals a tripartite structure: E→ℛ→CE \to \mathcal{R} \to C. Every element accesses a set of resources; every resource is governed by a set of change drivers; the element’s change-driver set is derived, not primitive:
Γ(e)=⋃r∈R(e)D(r) \Gamma(e) = \bigcup_{r \in R(e)} D(r) 
This is why the coupling-side and cohesion-side derivations are two ends of the same refinement chain: the resource-set partition refines the Γ partition. Γ is derived from RR through the governance mapping.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
section: 5 Coupling is a consequence of cohesion
text:
5 Coupling is a consequence of cohesion
The classical imperative — “maximize cohesion, minimize coupling” — treats the two as independent objectives requiring a trade-off. The series proves otherwise: within any single dimension, coupling is a consequence of cohesion, and the coupling categories that modularization controls are diagnostic of cohesion defects, not independent design variables.
Coupling decomposes into eight mutually exclusive categories — the product of three binary partitions (internal/external, same-class/cross-class, necessary/not), parameterized by a partitioning rule. At maximal cohesion (purity = completeness = 1), all modularization-controlled coupling categories are empty.
The result: the normative decomposition simultaneously maximizes cohesion and minimizes avoidable coupling — one optimum, not two.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
text:
6 The coupling floor
There is an irreducible coupling the domain demands — the coupling floor. At correct boundaries, the floor equals the necessary dependency graph exactly; every edge above it is a boundary defect or an accidental edge.
Because coupling is measured against a partitioning rule, necessary coupling is rule-relative: the same edge that one concern demands be internal is, under another, demanded external. The imperative to “minimize coupling” has no fixed referent until the rule is fixed. A raw count cannot separate domain-mandated coupling from placement error.

title: Coupling: Core Conclusions
text:
7 Where the proofs live
The proofs — that coupling is access to a shared resource, that the resource-set partition uniquely minimizes accidental coupling, that coupling is a consequence of cohesion, the coupling floor — are in the published coupling papers: the definition of coupling as shared resource access in the paper on the nature of coupling [1], the derivation of the modularisation directive from coupling in the derivation paper [2], and the coupling floor and coupling-as-consequence-of-cohesion results in the decomposition paper [3].

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
text:
Design dashboards like one number per module. Complexity, coupling, cohesion — a single score, a colour, a flag. This page shows why, for cohesion, one number cannot decide whether an element is well placed. The failure is not a matter of precision or of a poorly chosen formula. It is structural, and it has four independent causes.
A module can deviate from its rule in two opposite ways — it can hold elements that do not belong, or it can be missing elements that do. These two defects call for opposite repairs, and no single number can tell them apart. The rest of this page proves that claim and its companions.
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
text:
1 The setting
Cohesion is correctness relative to a partitioning rule [1]. A rule PP sorts the element set EE into equivalence classes [e]P[e]_P — the elements that belong together. A module M⊆EM \subseteq E complies when its boundary coincides with its class: M=[e]PM = [e]_P for every e∈Me \in M. Otherwise it deviates in one of two ways:

Impurity. MM contains elements from another class. The remedy is to remove them — to split.
Incompleteness. Some element of the module’s class lies outside MM. The remedy is to add it — to merge.

Assess a module MM against a class CC (the class it should realize). Write
purity(M)=|M∩C||M|,completeness(M)=|M∩C||C|.
\text{purity}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|M|},
\qquad
\text{completeness}(M) = \frac{|M \cap C|}{|C|}.

Both values lie in [0,1][0,1]. Purity is 11 exactly when MM has no foreign element; completeness is 11 exactly when MM is missing no member of CC. A module is fully cohesive precisely when both are 11.
The question of this page: can a single real number s(M)s(M) stand in for this pair and decide placement — issue the statement “this element is incorrectly placed”?
Two notions make the question precise.
Principled scalar. A function s(e,M,ℳ,E,R,P)→ℝs(e, M, \mathcal{M}, E, R, P) \to \mathbb{R} that may consult the principle PP as well as the structure — but whose output is one real number.
Verdict-deciding. ss decides placement iff there is an interpretation d:ℝ→{correct,incorrect}d: \mathbb{R} \to \{\text{correct}, \text{incorrect}\} with d(s(e,M))=VP(e,M)d(s(e,M)) = V_P(e,M) for every system and every element-module pair. (The module-level form s(M)s(M) is read the same way; the verdict is uniform across a module, so s(M)s(M) assigns one verdict to every element of MM.)
Four failure modes follow. They run from the strongest restriction on the metric — it cannot even see the rule — to the weakest — it sees everything and still adds nothing.
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 2 Failure mode 1 — the metric cannot see the rule
text:
2 Failure mode 1 — the metric cannot see the rule
Suppose the number is computed from the structure alone: from EE, RR, and the module MM, with no access to PP. Then it cannot decide placement, whatever its formula and whatever its precision.
Example. Let E={a,b}E = \{a, b\} and R=∅R = \emptyset, and let the module under test be M={a}M = \{a\}.

Under P1P_1 with a single class {a,b}\{a, b\}, we have [a]P1={a,b}≠M[a]_{P_1} = \{a,b\} \neq M, so aa is incorrectly placed (the module is missing bb).
Under P2P_2 with classes {a},{b}\{a\}, \{b\}, we have [a]P2={a}=M[a]_{P_2} = \{a\} = M, so aa is correctly placed.

The two systems present identical structural inputs — same EE, same RR, same MM — to any structural function, so such a function returns the same number for both. Yet the verdicts differ. No formula over the structure alone can be correct on both, at any level of precision.
This is the principle-blindness obstruction: the structure (E,R)(E,R) underdetermines PP, so “correct” — which is meaningless without PP — cannot be read off it. The constructive cell is also visible: give the metric access to PP and it can compare MM with [e]P[e]_P. But access alone is not enough, as the next three results show.
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 3 Failure mode 2 — one axis collapses two opposite defects
text:
3 Failure mode 2 — one axis collapses two opposite defects
Grant the metric full access to PP, but let it return one number per module, built from the two-axis pair: s(M)=g(purity(M),completeness(M))s(M) = g(\text{purity}(M), \text{completeness}(M)) for some g:[0,1]2→ℝg: [0,1]^2 \to \mathbb{R}.

Proposition (aggregation ambiguity). (a) If gg is symmetric — g(p,c)=g(c,p)g(p,c) = g(c,p) — there are two modules with opposite defects and opposite remedies whose scores are exactly equal. (b) If gg is continuous and strictly increasing in each argument, the two classes of defect are indistinguishable to any measurement precision, and no threshold on the score separates them.

Proof. Fix a rule PP with a class CC of size 44, and four foreign elements x1,…,x4x_1, \dots, x_4 all belonging to another class.

Let M1=C∪{x1,x2,x3,x4}M_1 = C \cup \{x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4\}, so |M1|=8|M_1| = 8. Then purity(M1)=4/8=1/2\text{purity}(M_1) = 4/8 = 1/2 and completeness(M1)=4/4=1\text{completeness}(M_1) = 4/4 = 1: impure but complete — the remedy is to remove the four foreign elements.
Let M2={a,b}M_2 = \{a, b\} for two elements a,b∈Ca, b \in C. Then purity(M2)=2/2=1\text{purity}(M_2) = 2/2 = 1 and completeness(M2)=2/4=1/2\text{completeness}(M_2) = 2/4 = 1/2: pure but incomplete — the remedy is to add the two missing members.

Both modules can be realized in one system (E,R,P)(E, R, P).
(a) By symmetry, s(M1)=g(1/2,1)=g(1,1/2)=s(M2)s(M_1) = g(1/2, 1) = g(1, 1/2) = s(M_2): the scores coincide exactly, while the defects and the required repairs are opposite. The geometric mean g(p,c)=pcg(p,c) = \sqrt{pc} scores both modules at 1/21/\sqrt{2}.
(b) Consider the two boundary curves B1={(p,1):0<p<1}B_1 = \{(p, 1) : 0 < p < 1\} (impure-but-complete) and B2={(1,c):0<c<1}B_2 = \{(1, c) : 0 < c < 1\} (pure-but-incomplete). Because gg is strictly increasing, g(1,1)g(1,1) is the supremum of gg on both curves; because gg is continuous, each image g(B1)g(B_1), g(B2)g(B_2) is an interval with that same supremum. Two intervals with a common supremum overlap: there exist (p*,1)∈B1(p^*, 1) \in B_1 and (1,c*)∈B2(1, c^*) \in B_2 with g(p*,1)=g(1,c*)g(p^*, 1) = g(1, c^*). So an impure-but-complete module and a pure-but-incomplete module share the same score, and in their neighbourhood the two classes of module are indistinguishable to any finite precision. An interpretation that reads the failure mode off intervals of the score line therefore misclassifies achievable modules — there is no threshold that separates “remove foreign elements” from “add missing members.” ◼\blacksquare
The single number says something is wrong. It cannot say what, and the two repairs point in opposite directions.

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 4 Failure mode 3 — a number cannot name the element
text:
4 Failure mode 3 — a number cannot name the element
Even a scalar that could read the defect from the score still could not say which element to move. Suppose ss is name-invariant: renaming the elements — carrying one system to another by a bijection σ\sigma with R′=σ(R)R' = \sigma(R), P′=σ∘P∘σ−1P' = \sigma \circ P \circ \sigma^{-1}, ℳ′=σ(ℳ)\mathcal{M}' = \sigma(\mathcal{M}) — leaves the score unchanged, sS′(σ(M))=sS(M)s_{S'}(\sigma(M)) = s_S(M). Any function deserving the name “measurement of the configuration” is name-invariant.

Proposition (no localization). A name-invariant module-level scalar cannot identify the repair target. There are two systems with the same element set, the same module MM, and the same score, whose minimal repairs move different elements.

Proof. Let E={a,b,c,x}E = \{a, b, c, x\}, let R=∅R = \emptyset, and let M={a,b,x}M = \{a, b, x\}.

System 1. P1P_1 induces classes {a,b}\{a, b\} and {c,x}\{c, x\}. Then MM is not a P1P_1-class, and the unique one-move repair is to remove xx: M\{x}={a,b}M \setminus \{x\} = \{a, b\} is a P1P_1-class, while no other single move produces one.
System 2. P2P_2 induces classes {a,x}\{a, x\} and {c,b}\{c, b\}. Again MM is not a class, and the unique one-move repair is to remove bb: M\{b}={a,x}M \setminus \{b\} = \{a, x\}.

Now take the transposition σ=(bx)\sigma = (b\ x), which exchanges bb and xx and fixes aa and cc. It carries system 1 to system 2: σ({a,b})={a,x}\sigma(\{a,b\}) = \{a,x\}, σ({c,x})={c,b}\sigma(\{c,x\}) = \{c,b\}, σ(R)=R\sigma(R) = R, and σ(M)=M\sigma(M) = M (the set {a,b,x}\{a,b,x\} is fixed as a set).
By name-invariance, sS2(M)=sS2(σ(M))=sS1(M)s_{S_2}(M) = s_{S_2}(\sigma(M)) = s_{S_1}(M): the score is the same in both systems. But the repair targets differ — xx in system 1, bb in system 2. A designer observing only the score cannot tell the two configurations apart. And the obstruction is structural, not a matter of resolution: a score fine-grained enough to point at xx rather than bb would have to change under the transposition σ\sigma — and would thereby cease to be name-invariant, that is, cease to measure the configuration. ◼\blacksquare

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 5 Failure mode 4 — a scalar that decides is the rule in disguise
text:
5 Failure mode 4 — a scalar that decides is the rule in disguise
The first three results say a measurement-like scalar fails. The fourth closes the other direction: a scalar that does decide placement adds nothing.

Proposition (degeneracy). Any scalar that decides placement is threshold-equivalent to the rule’s own binary verdict.

Proof. Suppose ss decides placement via dd, in either the element-level form s(e,M)s(e,M) or the module-level form s(M)s(M). Let T={x∈ℝ:d(x)=correct}T = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : d(x) = \text{correct}\}, the preimage of the “correct” verdict. Then, using the definition of the verdict, s(e,M)∈T⇔d(s(e,M))=correct⇔VP(e,M)=correct⇔M=[e]P.
s(e, M) \in T \iff d(s(e,M)) = \text{correct} \iff V_P(e,M) = \text{correct} \iff M = [e]_P .
 So the indicator 1[M=[e]P]1[M = [e]_P] is recovered from the scalar by a single threshold test. (For the module-level form, the same unfolding gives s(M)∈T⇔Ms(M) \in T \iff M is a PP-class, since the verdict is uniform across a module.)
The real-valued structure — magnitude, ordering, continuity, distance from the threshold — contributes nothing to the decision. Any two verdict-deciding scalars induce the same partition of element-module pairs, the partition the rule already defines: one scalar might use [0,1][0,1] with threshold 0.50.5, another ℝ\mathbb{R} with threshold 00, but the partition is identical. ◼\blacksquare
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 6 The four modes cover every scalar
text:
6 The four modes cover every scalar
The results assemble into a trichotomy. Every scalar aimed at the placement verdict either lacks the principle, has it but fails to decide, or decides only degenerately.

Principle-blind. No measurement without PP decides placement (failure mode 1).
Non-deciding. With PP, a scalar may fail to decide. For the measurement-like classes the failure is provable: a scalar factoring through the purity/completeness pair cannot determine the failure mode (failure mode 2), and a name-invariant scalar cannot identify the repair target (failure mode 3).
Degenerate. With PP, any scalar that decides placement is threshold-equivalent to the rule’s binary verdict (failure mode 4).

In every case the placement verdict originates in the partitioning rule, not in a number. A number can repeat the rule’s verdict on a module; only the rule can say what is wrong and which element must move.
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
section: 7 What the scalar is still good for — and what it is not
text:
7 What the scalar is still good for — and what it is not
The result is a limit on deciding. It does not by itself say that a scalar has no practical use — but the usual consolation is weaker than it sounds.
The consolation runs: even if a number cannot decide, it can rank modules for inspection — which to examine first, which grouping looks most suspect. But a ranking asks the scalar to do exactly what the proposition forbids: order modules by comparing an impurity defect with an incompleteness defect on a single line. Any such order presupposes an aggregate g(purity,completeness)g(\text{purity}, \text{completeness}) and, with it, an exchange rate between “an element that does not belong” and “a class member that is missing.” The two axes are independent and incommensurable; nothing in the rule or the domain fixes that rate. Change the aggregate — product, arithmetic mean, weighted sum — and the same modules are ordered differently: a designer ranking by pc\sqrt{pc} and one ranking by 0.7p+0.3c0.7p + 0.3c will name different modules as most suspect, and the rule adjudicates nothing between them.
So even the attention-directing use rests on a convention, not on cohesion. What survives without arbitration is only the degenerate bit: whether a module sits at (1,1)(1,1) or below it — the rule’s own verdict, reproduced by a threshold. Everything finer is a chosen weighting. A scalar score can therefore flag that a module is not a class, and a designer may adopt a heuristic order to decide where to look first — but the order is not grounded in the theory, is not invariant across aggregates, and two defensible scores need not agree.
A separate and weaker point concerns empirical use: structural scores have been reported to correlate with fault-proneness and maintenance effort, so they can serve as screening signals and change predictors. That is a statistical fact about a proxy for change, not a claim that the score measures cohesion — and it does not repair the arbitrariness of ranking by the score.
The impossibility still bites when the score is asked to issue the verdict — to declare an element misplaced from the number alone, without comparing the module against the rule. There, the score is not merely arbitrary; it is the rule in disguise.
crumbs: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric

title: Why Cohesion Has No Scalar Metric
text:
8 Where this comes from
The cohesion schema — correctness relative to a partitioning rule, and the (purity, completeness) pair — is defined and developed in On the Nature of Cohesion [1]. The constructive alternative it points to is the per-rule pair for diagnosis, and the rule PP itself for the verdict. The companion page Why two metrics are necessary proves that the pair is the minimal adequate output for a single rule.
