title: CUPID
text:
2 Composable
Composable is developed through three characteristics — a small surface area, intention-revealing naming, and minimal dependencies — under a governing statement: the characteristics “are neither necessary nor sufficient to make any guarantees”, and “more is not necessarily better; it is all trade-offs”, with a “sweet spot” between fragmented and bloated [1].
That caution is not, on its own, what makes the property hard to assess. A characteristic can be neither necessary nor sufficient and still support a graded comparison, provided the characteristics share an axis on which to order them. What blocks the comparison is that no such axis is supplied. “More is not necessarily better” denies that more of a characteristic means more of the property; the sweet spot is named but not measured; and the characteristics pull against one another, so improving one can worsen another. With no measure of the centre, a reviewer cannot decide how much of the property a component exhibits.

title: CUPID
text:
3 Unix philosophy
The Unix philosophy is glossed as “does one thing well”, grounded in the Unix tool tradition [1]. Its criterion is “a specific, well-defined, and comprehensive purpose”, and each adjective demands the judgment it is meant to guide. “Specific” and “well-defined” restate the goal — a clear boundary — without a test for when the boundary is clear. “Comprehensive” requires the purpose to be broad enough to be complete yet narrow enough to remain one, with no way to tell when it is broad enough. The example illustrates a design judgment and supplies no test: a designer who kept two tools together would still satisfy the criterion. The property therefore gives no rule for when a purpose counts as one and comprehensive enough.

title: CUPID
text:
4 Predictable
Predictable is glossed as “does what you expect”, with three sub-properties: it should behave as expected, be deterministic, and be observable [1].
Determinism and observability can be assessed against a specification the reviewer states from the component itself — determinism against its functional bounds, observability against a stated output-and-state specification. The headline sub-property is different. “Behaves as expected” is relative to an observer the essay does not fix: obviousness is held by a reader, and readers differ. Its own example — confidence in a low-coverage trading codebase — reports a judgment, not a measure, and credits two properties at once [1]. Predictable is therefore assessable in its deterministic and observable sub-properties, but not in its headline gloss.

title: CUPID
text:
5 Idiomatic
Idiomatic is glossed as “feels natural”, defined against a target audience: an experienced programmer fluent in the language, its libraries, its toolchain, and its ecosystem [1].
How much a reviewer can assess depends on the language. Some languages have strong opinions about how code should look, and a canonical formatter settles syntactic quirks — though idioms reach further than the language definition. Others are deliberately multi-paradigm, where it is left to the team to decide what good looks like [1]. The standard comes from a language community, a tool, or the team, never from CUPID, which supplies the name and the observation that consistency matters but no standard against which idiomaticness is judged.

title: CUPID
text:
6 Domain-based
Domain-based is glossed as “the solution domain models the problem domain in language and structure”, with three parts: language, structure, and boundaries [1].
The advice is actionable: grouping a design by use case rather than by technical type, because type-grouping scatters a change across the codebase [1]. Whether the property lets a reviewer decide how much of it the code exhibits is a narrower question, and it is not answered. All three parts take “the domain” as given: identifying it, and deciding where its parts divide, is the hard problem, and no criterion is given for it. The worked example names several areas but no rule for finding them; a different designer could name others. The level of boundary is likewise left to the judgment the property is meant to guide, and the success criterion — that a casual observer cannot tell whether people are discussing the code or the domain — describes an outcome, not a test [1].

title: CUPID
section: 7 The set against its own criteria
text:
7 The set against its own criteria
The articulation leg of the practical criterion is met: each property is stated in a sentence, with examples and counterexamples [1]. The human criterion is met: the five names are chosen for the perspective of people, not code. The assessment leg is not met for the property as a whole, and the adoption leg does not compensate — a direction whose centre the property does not locate is easy to adopt for the same reason it is hard to assess.
The layered criterion holds in form only. The depth is real, but it is the same content whose assessment fails, so it adds no independent support.
Terhorst-North makes two remarks about how the properties combine: that everything is a trade-off, so context should always be considered; and that the properties are mutually reinforcing [1]. Both can hold, but the essay does not join them, and states no procedure for the case the first describes — two properties pulling in opposite directions on the same code.
What the analysis leaves is a vocabulary and a stance: memorable names for outcomes practitioners value, and guidance as a centre to move towards, with no gate to pass. None of the five properties meets the assessment requirement as a whole.

title: CUPID
text:
8 Beyond the author’s criteria
The assessment above used Terhorst-North’s criteria, and is confined to them. That method cannot place CUPID against the standards of a technical discipline, because the properties answer to no standard outside the essay. Two standards define engineering practice: grounding in a theory or a model [6], [7], [8], and falsifiability [9].
On grounding, the five properties are selected, not derived. They were chosen because they “feel foundational” and stated as beliefs and preferences, with no model, theory, or empirical result behind them [1]. The choice is arbitrary on its own account — CUPID is a backronym, and several candidates existed for each letter — so there is no principled reason to prefer these five [1].
On falsifiability, a claim is falsifiable when some observation could refute it [9]. The properties are stated as centres, and the trade-off remark answers any apparent violation: a codebase that appears to violate a property is either a trade-off or too far from the centre, never a counterexample [1]. No observation can fail a property, and none can be checked against a model because none is offered.
As a replacement for SOLID, CUPID also fails on coverage. SOLID poses five design questions — responsibility boundary, extension, substitutability, interface granularity, dependency direction — and a replacement should engage the same questions [10]. It does not: only the Unix philosophy approaches one, single purpose, and even that is presented as a different, outside-in property [1]. Nothing in the five says how to extend a design, when a substitution is sound, how to split an interface, or which way a dependency should point. The packaging principles that accompany SOLID are untouched as well [10].
The expected reply is that CUPID never claimed to be rigorous, so this section attacks a claim its author does not make. That is correct, and the objection is not to CUPID’s informality. It is to the opposite move: presenting the properties as a replacement for SOLID, and claiming an effect — that the more code has these qualities, the more joyful it is to work with [1] — while disclaiming the standards on which design guidance is judged. The disclaimer cannot have it both ways: if CUPID claims no results and no grounds, it can claim neither to replace SOLID nor to improve anything.

title: CUPID
text:
9 What remains
On its author’s own terms, CUPID fails the assessment requirement he set: the articulation and human criteria are met, the assessment requirement fails for Composable and the Unix philosophy, holds only in part for Predictable, holds for Idiomatic only against an external standard, and has no criterion for Domain-based, while layering adds no independent support [1].
On the standards that define engineering [6], [7], [8], the five properties rest on no model or result and are not falsifiable [9], so they give no basis for expecting improvement. The result is narrow: it does not say the five names are useless, that the recommendations behind them are unsound, or that CUPID is worse than SOLID. Several recommendations have merit on their own — narrow interfaces, observability, domain language, consistent formatting.
What CUPID is, on its own presentation, is a statement of what its author values in code, with no result demonstrated [1]. It belongs to a third category — practitioner advice — legitimate, but neither engineering nor science, and with no reason to believe it is right.

title: PL/SQL (Oracle)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 46/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 61/100
Core Coupling Analysis: PL/SQL (Procedural Language for SQL) is Oracle’s procedural extension for SQL, modeled on Ada and Pascal. Its best coupling feature is the package, which separates a specification (the interface: types, variables, constants, exceptions, cursors, subprograms) from an optional body (the implementation), enabling encapsulation and function overloading. Blocks with DECLARE/BEGIN/EXCEPTION/END provide structured error handling, and user-defined and predefined exceptions make failure explicit. Its coupling weaknesses are those of its domain: everything is coupled to the Oracle database engine, variables default to NULL, and triggers create implicit coupling by firing automatically in response to data changes. Dynamic SQL (via EXECUTE IMMEDIATE or DBMS_SQL) couples code to string-built queries and carries injection risk. Package variables have session scope, which can create hidden shared state. It is not a general-purpose language; it only makes sense inside an Oracle database.
Platform & Ecosystem: PL/SQL is ubiquitous in Oracle enterprise systems and has been since Oracle 6 (stored procedures since 7), so the ecosystem and tooling are mature. It implements the ISO SQL/PSM standard and is also available in TimesTen and IBM Db2. Evolution is tied to Oracle’s release cadence. It is strongly coupled to Oracle and porting to other databases (e.g., SQL Server’s Transact-SQL) is non-trivial because of differences in features and in concurrency and locking models. The learning curve is moderate for developers who know SQL and a Pascal-like language. Security is reasonable with proper bind variables, but dynamic SQL is a classic SQL-injection surface.

title: SAS (9.4 / Viya)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 51/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 54/100
Core Coupling Analysis: SAS is a proprietary data-analysis and AI platform whose language has a genuinely distinctive feature: the strict separation between the DATA step (which retrieves and manipulates data) and PROC steps (which analyze and report on it) — a genuine separation of data-handling concerns from analysis concerns. Beyond that, SAS is weak on coupling separation: data is organized into datasets (tables of observations and variables) rather than general typed values, there is no general-purpose type system or modules beyond macros, and there are no structured exceptions. Macros (pieces of code or variables coded once and referenced for repetitive tasks) can create macro-expansion coupling. Everything is proprietary and tied to SAS datasets and the SAS Institute toolchain. The point-and-click Enterprise Guide interface hides the language entirely for non-technical users.
Platform & Ecosystem: SAS was the leading advanced-analytics platform for decades — the largest market-share holder in advanced analytics (35.4% in 2013) and widely used in finance, insurance, government, healthcare, and clinical trials (the FDA historically required NDA submissions in the SAS XPORT transport format, since largely superseded by CDISC standards). However, it faces strong competition from R and Python, which are cheaper and open source. SAS is proprietary and expensive (subscription-based), and the language has evolved slowly; SAS Viya (2016) modernized the architecture and added cloud and open-source interop (R, Python, Jupyter) without positioning as a replacement for SAS 9.4. The learning curve is steep, the DATA-step syntax is idiosyncratic, and the ecosystem is large but closed. It remains powerful for regulated statistical work but is increasingly a legacy choice.

title: Transact-SQL (SQL Server)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 65/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 69/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Transact-SQL (T-SQL) is the procedural extension to SQL used by Microsoft SQL Server and SAP Adaptive Server Enterprise. Like PL/SQL, it couples application logic directly to the database engine. Stored procedures provide modularity and can return status values and output parameters. TRY...CATCH gives structured exception handling. Local variables (declared with DECLARE @name) default to NULL, and NULL handling pervades the language. Triggers create implicit coupling by firing on data changes. T-SQL is fundamentally distinct from PL/SQL despite superficial similarity — porting between them requires non-trivial work, because of feature differences and of deeper differences in how Oracle and SQL Server handle concurrency and locking. There is no general type system beyond SQL data types; everything is data-centric.
Platform & Ecosystem: Transact-SQL is deeply embedded in the Microsoft enterprise data stack (SQL Server, Azure SQL) and in SAP ASE, giving it a large, mature ecosystem. Microsoft and SAP maintain separate documentation. Evolution follows the SQL Server release cadence, which is regular and active. It is strongly vendor-locked to the Microsoft/SAP database world. The learning curve is moderate for SQL developers, and tooling (SSMS, Azure Data Studio) is good. Security is reasonable with parameterized queries, but string-built dynamic SQL and legacy cursor patterns carry injection and coupling risk. Its niche is transactional and analytical logic that must live inside SQL Server or SAP ASE.

title: D (2.112)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 61/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 92/100
Core Coupling Analysis: D is a systems language designed as a successor to C++, offering optional garbage collection alongside manual memory management. Its templates are more readable than C++ templates, avoiding the notorious angle-bracket verbosity. D’s module system decouples compilation units more cleanly than C++ headers, eliminating the need for include guards. UFCS (Universal Function Call Syntax) allows method-call syntax on any type without requiring the method to be defined inside the type, decoupling syntax from definition site. Contract programming with in, out, and invariant blocks separates preconditions, postconditions, and invariants from implementation logic. The @safe, @trusted, and @system attributes separate memory-safety guarantees at the function level. CTFE (Compile-Time Function Execution) decouples metaprogramming from runtime overhead by allowing arbitrary functions to execute during compilation. BetterC mode supports embedded and no-GC environments. D supports multiple paradigms: imperative, object-oriented, functional, and metaprogramming.
Platform & Ecosystem: D follows a design philosophy summarized as “Better C++”: it provides C++-level performance and low-level control while simplifying the language with cleaner templates, a proper module system, no preprocessor, and both garbage collected and manual memory management options. Its ecosystem is smaller than Rust or C++ and its adoption remains niche rather than mainstream. Performance is excellent because D compiles to native code; the reference compiler dmd uses its own Digital-Mars backend, while the alternative compilers ldc (LLVM) and gdc (GCC) provide LLVM- and GCC-based backends. BetterC mode targets embedded systems and no-garbage-collection environments. The learning curve is moderate for developers familiar with C++. Tooling is improving, with dub as the standard package manager. The syntax is cleaner than C++ while providing similar expressive power. D is a good fit for game development, and the vibe.d framework supports web development. Corporate backing is weak, and the community is small but dedicated.

title: JavaScript (ES2025)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

❌ No static types: All coupling deferred to runtime
✅ Prototypes decouple: Can modify behavior without inheritance
⚠️ Duck typing: Structural at runtime, but no safety
❌ Type coercion couples: Implicit conversions hide intent

Object Construction:

✅ Object literals: Simple construction without classes
⚠️ Prototypes flexible: Can change after construction
❌ new keyword confusing: this binding couples to call context
⚠️ Factory functions decouple: Can avoid new entirely

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory: Generational GC (implementation dependent)
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: V8, SpiderMonkey, etc. have different characteristics
❌ Closure captures create leaks: Easy to accidentally hold references
❌ Event listener leaks common: Forgotten listeners prevent collection
❌ DOM circular references: Event handlers can create uncollectable cycles
⚠️ WeakMap/WeakRef help: Can create weak references, but not automatic

Error Handling:

❌ Exceptions unchecked: No type tracking
❌ Promise rejection unchecked: .catch() optional
⚠️ Result types possible: Libraries exist but uncommon
❌ Callbacks couple error/success: (err, result) mixes concerns

Concurrency:

✅ Event loop implicit: Single-threaded simplifies
✅ Async/await separates: Explicit async functions
❌ Promise errors untracked: Rejection type unknown
⚠️ Web Workers separate: Explicit message passing, but manual

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Global scope couples: window, globalThis everywhere
❌ Module side effects: Import order matters
❌ this binding couples: Context depends on call site
❌ Undefined/null confusion: Two absence types couple
❌ Prototype pollution: Can modify built-in prototypes globally

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Dynamic Typing vs. Predictability: All coupling deferred to runtime, no compile-time detection
Flexibility vs. Correctness: Can modify anything at runtime, couples correctness to discipline
Type Coercion: Implicit conversions couple values to contexts ("5" + 3 === "53", "5" - 3 === 2)
This Binding: Function context couples to call site (.call(), .apply(), .bind() required)
Callback Hell vs. Promises vs. Async/Await: Three async paradigms couple code to era written
Module Systems: CommonJS vs. ES6 modules couples code to environment (Node vs. browser)
Prototype Chain: Inheritance couples objects to prototype chain modifications

Core Coupling Score: 28/100

Score

Verdict: JavaScript’s dynamic nature defers all coupling detection to runtime. Prototypes and object literals provide flexibility but no guarantees. Global scope and unchecked errors create pervasive coupling. Main strength: object literals and prototypes are simple. Main weakness: no type system means coupling invisible until runtime.

❌ @ operator suppresses errors: Hides coupling
⚠️ Modern frameworks handle better: Laravel/Symfony impose discipline

⚠️ Request-per-process prevents some coupling: But wastes resources

title: Ruby (4.0)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

❌ Duck typing: No compile-time type checking, coupling invisible
✅ Pattern matching (3.0+): case/in provides exhaustive structural matching
✅ Mixins: Include modules for behavior without inheritance
⚠️ Open classes: Can modify any class, creates action-at-a-distance coupling
⚠️ RBS type signatures: External type system (.rbs files) — static checking via Steep/Sorbet, not built into runtime
✅ Blocks/Procs/Lambdas: First-class functions decouple behavior

Object Construction:

✅ initialize separate from new: Construction logic decoupled
✅ Data.define (3.2+): Immutable value objects like records/kotlin data classes
⚠️ Class methods for factories: Common pattern but not enforced
❌ No validation enforcement: Constructor invariants not checked

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Garbage collection: Automatic, no manual management
⚠️ GC pauses: Non-deterministic, couples performance to runtime (improved by YJIT’s reduced allocation rate)
✅ No manual deallocation: Can’t have use-after-free
✅ YJIT reduces GC pressure: Faster execution means fewer long-lived allocations

Error Handling:

❌ Unchecked exceptions: raise doesn’t appear in signatures
❌ Broad rescue: rescue without type catches everything
✅ Pattern matching with => operator (3.0+): Can destructure error objects structurally
❌ Silent failures: Methods often return nil instead of raising

Concurrency:

❌ Global VM Lock (GVL): Like Python’s GIL, couples threads to single core
✅ Fibers + Fiber Scheduler (3.0+): Cooperative concurrency with io_uring support for async I/O
✅ M:N thread scheduler (3.3+, experimental → progressing): Lightweight userspace threads
⚠️ Ractors: Actor-like concurrency (3.0+), still evolving
❌ Shared mutable state: No protection, race conditions easy

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Monkey patching: Can modify any class anywhere, global coupling
❌ Global variables: $global creates pervasive coupling
❌ Class variables: @@var shared across all instances, couples classes
❌ Method_missing: Dynamic dispatch hides coupling, runtime failures
❌ Open classes: Modification anywhere affects everywhere

title: Assembly (x86-64, System V AMD64 ABI)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 17/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 58/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Assembly provides complete control over the machine, decoupling the programmer from any abstraction layer — because none exist. Registers are effectively global mutable state shared by all instructions. Labels couple jump and call targets to specific memory addresses within the code. Macros decouple repetitive instruction sequences by allowing the programmer to define reusable code blocks. Calling conventions couple function calls to a specific ABI (Application Binary Interface), tying code to a particular platform’s register and stack usage conventions. Platform-specific instructions couple the program to a particular CPU architecture. The absence of types couples everything to the programmer’s discipline: a register can hold an integer, a pointer, or garbage, and nothing checks which is intended.
Platform & Ecosystem: Assembly is used for performance-critical kernels, embedded systems, and reverse engineering where no higher-level language provides sufficient control. The learning curve is extremely steep: the programmer must understand registers, instruction sets, and the target platform’s ABI. There are no abstractions. Syntax varies significantly between Intel and AT&T dialects even for the same instruction set. Everything is manual. Security guarantees are nonexistent: all classic vulnerabilities (buffer overflows, use-after-free, return-oriented programming) are possible and nothing prevents them. Assembly is used only where C is too high-level.

text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 69/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 84/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Sound null safety (Dart 2.12+) — String vs String? like Kotlin, enforced at compile time. Strong static typing with type inference. No checked exceptions (like C#). Async/await with Future<T> separates sync from async. Isolates decouple concurrency (no shared memory, message-passing only). Sealed classes (Dart 3) for exhaustive pattern matching. Records (Dart 3) for structural data. Pattern matching (Dart 3) decouples destructuring. Extension methods decouple behavior from types. late keyword for lazy initialization decouples initialization from construction. text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 69/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 76/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Actor model decouples processes by design — no shared memory, message passing only. “Let it crash” philosophy decouples error handling from business logic via OTP (Open Telecom Platform) supervision trees. Pattern matching on binaries and messages exhaustively separates cases. Immutable data by default avoids mutation coupling. Hot code swapping decouples deployment from runtime, allowing upgrades without restarting the system. The ecosystem includes Hex.pm for packages, rebar3 and mix for builds, and growing tooling. Elixir’s ecosystem is accessible via Erlang interop. Performance is excellent for I/O-bound workloads but weak for CPU-bound computation. The actor concurrency model is widely regarded as the gold standard. The syntax is Prolog-derived and unfamiliar to most developers. The learning curve is steep, combining functional programming, the actor model, and OTP.

text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 58/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 61/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Solidity is a statically typed, ECMAScript-syntax language for writing smart contracts that run on the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM). Its coupling profile is tightly constrained by its domain. Contracts are the unit of encapsulation, and the language supports inheritance, including multiple inheritance with C3 linearization. It has complex member variables (hierarchical mappings and structs) and a type-safe ABI for multiple functions per contract. But coupling is pervasive and domain-specific: the blockchain context injects globals like msg.sender into every contract, coupling logic to the calling account. require/revert/errors make failure explicit but are not a general exception system. The EVM is single-threaded with gas accounting, so there is no concurrency in the usual sense and execution is tightly coupled to gas limits. Solidity has been criticized for being error-prone and for lacking constructs to handle blockchain-specific concerns, and its Turing-completeness means arbitrary-property verification cannot be automated decidably.
Platform & Ecosystem: Solidity is the primary language for Ethereum and other EVM-compatible blockchains, so it has a substantial young ecosystem (Foundry, Hardhat, Truffle). But it is niche, young, and carries significant security risk — it was partly blamed for The DAO hack (2016), and the smart-contract domain is rife with reentrancy and other vulnerabilities that are hard to reason about. Performance is poor in general-computing terms (EVM is slow and gas-metered). The language evolves actively (0.8.x releases), and static typing helps, but the tooling and security story remain immature relative to general-purpose languages. It is the right tool only for on-chain smart contracts; outside that domain it has no value.

title: COBOL (ISO/IEC 1989:2023)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 54/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 54/100
Core Coupling Analysis: COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language) is a compiled, English-like language that has dominated business, finance, and mainframe systems since 1960. Its most coupling-relevant feature is the strict four-division structure — Identification, Environment, Data, and Procedure — which genuinely separates data definition from program logic. The Data Division declares data hierarchically via level-numbers and the PICTURE clause. But COBOL’s coupling profile is weak: typing is weak and static (numeric data converts silently between representations; alphanumeric data can be placed in any item that holds strings), the standard specifies no large library (43 statements, 87 functions, one class), and PERFORM provides no parameter passing or call stack. Pre-COBOL-85, a procedure could access and modify any data item — access restriction was impossible. GO TO promotes spaghetti code, and COBOL programs are infamous for being monolithic and hard to modularize. Exceptions are handled by declaratives and may not terminate the program. The result is a language whose local readability masks pervasive global coupling.
Platform & Ecosystem: COBOL remains among the most widely deployed languages: Gartner reported over 200 billion lines in 1997, and COBOL still runs background processes for most credit/debit-card swipes. The 2023 standard (ISO/IEC 1989:2023) added asynchronous messaging, transaction processing, and other modern features, and GnuCOBOL (a standalone open-source compiler, distinct from GCC) implements it. However, the ecosystem is legacy and vendor-fragmented (IBM, Micro Focus, GnuCOBOL), evolution is glacial, and the skills base is shrinking due to retirements (a problem highlighted during the COVID-era unemployment-systems crisis). It is superb for its niche — high-volume batch and transaction processing on mainframes — but poor for nearly everything else. The learning curve is steep in practice because of verbosity and over 300 reserved words.

title: Objective-C (2.0)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 42/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 65/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Objective-C is a strict superset of C that adds Smalltalk-style message passing. Its central coupling characteristic is dynamic messaging: the target of a message is resolved at runtime, and the message-passing system has no type checking. This defers coupling detection to runtime — an object can be sent a message not in its interface, and message forwarding or nil-message handling then applies. But Objective-C also offers strong decoupling tools. Categories add methods to existing classes without subclassing or source access, enabling open classes. Protocols (formal interfaces, informal via categories) provide multiple inheritance of specification without implementation. Blocks (closures) decouple callbacks. Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) removes the manual retain/release memory-management coupling. Static typing information can optionally be added for compile-time checks. The main coupling weaknesses are the lack of namespaces (forcing prefix conventions prone to collision), dynamic dispatch that blocks optimization, and dynamic typing that can couple correctness to runtime.
Platform & Ecosystem: Objective-C was Apple’s primary language for macOS and iOS from the 1997 NeXT acquisition until Swift in 2014. It remains deeply embedded in the Cocoa and Cocoa Touch APIs and a huge amount of legacy Apple code. Implementations include Apple’s Clang (most complete, as of 2026), GCC, and GNUstep/libobjc2 for porting. Ecosystem and tooling are excellent within Apple’s platform but largely locked to it. The language is essentially frozen in favor of Swift. Performance is good (thin C runtime, compiled) but dynamic dispatch limits optimization relative to C++. Memory safety is strong under ARC, though dynamic typing and the generic id object pointer create some type-confusion risk. Learning the message-passing syntax is a barrier for developers from other OO languages.

title: VBScript (6.0)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 40/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 39/100
Core Coupling Analysis: VBScript (Visual Basic Scripting Edition) is Microsoft’s COM-based scripting language modeled on classic Visual Basic. Its coupling profile is weak by design. Variables default to the Variant type (weak, dynamic typing), so type coupling is deferred entirely to runtime, and VBScript deliberately omits strong typing, extended error trapping, and the ability to pass a variable number of parameters. Procedures and subroutines provide some modularity, and version 5.0 added classes and regular expressions. Windows Script Files (.wsf) allow modular reuse of multiple script files. But error handling is minimal, everything is coupled to the Windows COM object model, and the language cannot compose cleanly. It is easy to learn but provides almost no structural enforcement against coupling.
Platform & Ecosystem: VBScript was widely used by system administrators and in Internet Explorer, ASP, and HTML Applications, but it has been in decline for years and was officially deprecated by Microsoft in October 2023, with removal planned after 2027. Microsoft recommends migrating to PowerShell or JavaScript. It is Windows-bound and tied to COM (WSH, WMI, ADO). The ecosystem is legacy and largely frozen since 1998. Security is a concern: VBScript was the vehicle for the ILOVEYOU worm and other malware, and it is often blocked. It still appears in test automation (UFT One) and some embedded operator interfaces, but PowerShell has overwhelmingly replaced it.

title: The Great Language Smackdown: 65 Languages Through the Coupling Lens
text:
2 What is coupling?

2.1 A coupling taxonomy: accidental vs. necessary
Coupling falls into two fundamental kinds:








Kind
Definition
Origin




Necessary coupling
Dependencies the system cannot function without — the irreducible coupling floor. Causal dependencies dictated by the domain structure.
Domain artifacts


Accidental coupling
Dependencies that are not causally required — coupling that exists by developer choice, oversight, or language/platform constraint.
Design or platform



In any system, necessary coupling is the minimum possible: the inter-module communication the domain demands. Accidental coupling is everything beyond that — coupling introduced by design choice, oversight, or the language and platform itself. This taxonomy, and the coupling-floor idea it rests on, follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [11].
Accidental coupling subdivides into two subtypes, which are the core of this language analysis:








Subtype
Definition
Fix




Avoidable accidental
Could be removed by better design within the language’s capabilities. The developer chose to couple unnecessarily.
Better design


Language-imposed
Unavoidable given the language’s constructs — the irreducible residuum of accidental coupling the language inflicts on all programs. Even optimal design cannot eliminate it.
Change language or version



A language can also couple elements in dimensions beyond structural dependency. Coupling has several dimensions: structural, temporal, concurrency, security, platform, and language (memory model, type system, module system). Each dimension carries its own dependency relation, and coupling decomposes into necessary, spurious, and accidental components.
What this means for language comparison: This article evaluates languages along the language coupling dimension: how much language-imposed coupling does the language generate, and how well does it help you detect and eliminate avoidable accidental coupling? A language with a good coupling profile (a) minimizes language-imposed coupling (fewer constructs that force accidental edges) and (b) detects avoidable coupling at the earliest possible stage (compile time > static analysis > runtime > never).
This article’s scores answer: how close does this language let you get to the irreducible coupling floor?

title: The Great Language Smackdown: 65 Languages Through the Coupling Lens
text:
3 How We Score: Methodology
Every language imposes some amount of accidental coupling that even optimal design cannot eliminate. Headers force compilation coupling. Unchecked null forces null-check coupling. A global interpreter lock forces concurrency coupling. Dynamic typing forces coupling detection to runtime. These are not design mistakes — they are language properties.
Our scores are computed by an objective, reproducible algorithm, not by subjective impression:

A closed mechanism inventory — each coupling mechanism has a fixed weight.
A binary presence check — for each language, each mechanism is marked present or absent (a factual determination, not a severity judgment).
An arithmetic rule — within each dimension the present weights are summed and capped at −15 (one severe mechanism’s worth), and the score is 100 − Σ(capped per-dimension contributions).

Because the weights are fixed and the only per-language step is present/absent, any two analysts following these rules reach identical scores. The framework makes disagreement precise: to dispute a score, you must either contest a mechanism’s presence in a specific language, or propose changing a fixed weight and then recompute.
The full mechanism inventory (Core: Type, Construction, Memory, Error, Concurrency, Platform; Meta: Performance, Ecosystem, Evolution, Domain, Learning, Syntax, Testing, Security), the detailed capped-sum rule, the per-dimension sub-scores, and the complete per-language mechanism-presence data for all 65 languages — so any score can be reproduced from first principles — are in the companion article: The Objective Coupling Scoring Model: Full Mechanism Data for 65 Languages.

3.1 What the score means
Because the model is a fixed-inventory capped-sum-per-dimension model, the bands follow directly from the mechanism weights:

90+: No dimension contains a severe (High) mechanism, and at most one dimension reaches even −8. Near the irreducible floor.
75–89: No dimension reaches −15; a small number of moderate (−8) mechanisms spread across dimensions.
60–74: At least one dimension caps at −15 (a severe mechanism), or several dimensions carry moderate mechanisms.
45–59: Two or three dimensions cap at −15, or one severe mechanism plus several moderate across other dimensions.
Below 45: Three or more dimensions cap at −15 — the language’s design trades separation of concerns for other goals (simplicity, flexibility, ubiquity, or direct hardware access).

Performance (Coupling to Runtime Behavior) - High score = Predictable, deterministic performance - Low score = Unpredictable GC, runtime surprises couple logic to performance

Language Evolution (Coupling to Language Versions) - High score = Backward compatible, stable, no breaking changes - Low score = Frequent breaking changes couple codebase to specific versions
Domain Suitability (Coupling to Problem Domains) - High score = Works well across multiple domains - Low score = Couples to specific domains, struggles outside comfort zone
Learning Curve (Coupling Productivity to Expertise) - High score = Gentle, quick to productivity - Low score = Steep, productivity couples to deep expertise
Syntax & Ergonomics (Coupling Intent to Verbose Expression) - High score = Concise, readable, minimal boilerplate - Low score = Verbose, boilerplate couples intent to ceremony
Testing & Debugging (Coupling Understanding to Manual Inspection) - High score = Excellent tools, easy to test/debug - Low score = Poor tools couple understanding to manual inspection

By Paradigm: - Type System Powerhouses → Maximum safety, steep learning curves - Modern Mainstream → Best balance for most projects - Systems and Performance → When you need low-level control - Dynamic and Scripting → Rapid prototyping, flexibility over safety - Domain-Specific → Perfect fit for specialized problems
By Score (latest version, modern idioms): - 90+ (Elite): Rust — Near-zero language-imposed coupling; the sole language with no severe coupling mechanism in any dimension - 75-89 (Excellent): Swift, Unison, Ada, SQL, Rocq, SPARK, Lean4, Haskell — Strong languages; at most one severe mechanism, otherwise clean - 60-74 (Good): Zig, PureScript, OCaml, TypeScript, Transact-SQL, Elixir, Erlang, Dart, Clojure, Racket, Scheme, Kotlin, Nim, D, Crystal — Moderate coupling; real costs in at least one dimension - 45-59 (Fair): Go, Solidity, Tcl, Scala, F#, Delphi, Prolog, Scratch, C++, COBOL, Eiffel, Groovy, Java, C#, SAS, Smalltalk, Common Lisp, Visual Basic, PL/SQL, Turbo Pascal, R — Significant forced coupling; discipline and tooling compensate - <45 (Limited): Objective-C, PowerShell, Lua, Bash, Zsh, Ksh, Sh, C shell, Fish, VBScript, MATLAB, Julia, JavaScript, Python, PHP, Ruby, Perl, Fortran, C, Assembly — Pervasive forced coupling; legacy, domain-specific, or dynamically-typed

text:
17 The Verdict: Coupling Edition
Scores from the objective model (capped-sum-per-dimension), analysis date June 2026. Older versions of the same language can score significantly lower (e.g., C++98, Java 8).
If you need mathematical proof of correctness: Rocq (85), SPARK (85), Lean4 (85)
If you want bulletproof low coupling by language design: Rust (96), Swift (88), Unison (88), Ada (88)
If you want low coupling with pragmatism: Haskell (80), Zig (73), PureScript (73), OCaml (72), TypeScript (70)
If you want low coupling with discipline (modern versions): Erlang (69), Elixir (69), Dart (69), Transact-SQL (65), Clojure (62), Kotlin (61), Go (58)
Low coupling on a budget (ecosystem-driven): Tcl (58), F# (57), Delphi (57), Scala (57), C++ (54), Groovy (53)
Specialized excellence (unique coupling profiles): Erlang (69): Actor model with per-process isolation and let-it-crash. Elixir (69): Modern BEAM with macros and protocols. Julia (39): Multiple dispatch without inheritance. Eiffel (53): Design by Contract makes change drivers explicit and coupling across them detectable. Objective-C (42): Dynamic messaging plus categories, protocols, and blocks for decoupling. Turbo Pascal (46): Units give genuine interface/implementation separation rare among 1980s languages.
Domain-locked procedural database logic: PL/SQL (46) and Transact-SQL (65) couple all logic to their database engines but offer real encapsulation (packages/spec-body, stored procedures) and structured exceptions. SAS (51) uniquely separates the DATA step from PROC steps. Use them only where the logic must live inside the database or analytics engine.
Lowest forced coupling: 1. Rust (96): Ownership enforces separation, Result types compose, no null, traits decouple 2. Swift (88): Protocol-oriented design, value types, ARC 3. Unison (88): Content-addressed code, algebraic effects, distributed computing built-in 4. Ada (88): Strong static typing, packages, tasking, contracts 5. SQL (85): Declarative, no in-language coupling among your elements
Low coupling with pragmatism (latest versions): 1. Haskell (80): Type classes, explicit effects, immutability 2. Zig (73): Explicit everything, error unions, allocator parameters, comptime 3. PureScript (73): Effect system separates effect types 4. OCaml (72): Module system, immutable data, exhaustive pattern matching 5. TypeScript (70): Gradual typing adds compile-time detection incrementally
Highest forced coupling: 1. Assembly (17): No abstractions, manual everything, maximum coupling risk 2. C (25): Manual memory, weak typing, global state, undefined behavior 3. JavaScript (28): Dynamic, global state, unchecked errors, no types 4. PHP (28): Dynamic, weak typing, superglobals, no concurrency 5. Perl (28): Dynamic, global state, primitive objects, GIL
Neither helps nor hinders coupling: - C (25): With discipline, coupling can be low; without it, coupling is extreme - D (61): Better C++ with cleaner templates, contracts, and both GC and manual memory

title: The Great Language Smackdown: 65 Languages Through the Coupling Lens
text:
18 The Real Truth
Coupling scores depend heavily on which version of a language you’re using. C++23 is a fundamentally different language from C++98. Java 26 with records, sealed classes, and virtual threads is not the same as Java 8. Always check the version baseline.
Version aside, Coupling scores don’t determine project success. Context matters:

Team expertise trumps language coupling score
Ecosystem maturity often beats language elegance
Hiring availability is a real constraint
Performance requirements eliminate choices
Platform constraints narrow the field

But here’s what coupling analysis reveals:
Languages with proven separation (Lean4, Rocq, SPARK) mathematically guarantee correctness. Extreme learning curve, but zero-defect systems achievable.
Languages with enforced separation (Rust, Haskell, PureScript, OCaml) make coupling impossible to hide. You pay upfront in learning curve, gain long-term in maintainability.
Languages with optional separation (Swift, Kotlin, C#, TypeScript, modern Java, modern C++, Eiffel, Groovy) let you choose coupling level. Good for migration, requires discipline.
Languages with manual separation (C, D, Zig, COBOL, Turbo Pascal) give you rope to hang yourself or build elegantly. Expertise required.
Languages with runtime-only separation (JavaScript, Python, PHP, Ruby, shells, VBScript) defer most coupling detection to testing — but Python 3.14 (free-threaded), PHP 8.4 (property hooks, fibers), and Ruby 4.0 (YJIT, pattern matching) have all made meaningful coupling-separation progress in recent versions.
Languages with domain-locked separation (Objective-C, PL/SQL, Transact-SQL, SAS, Solidity) are coupled to a single platform or domain — the platform is the unit boundary, and the language’s coupling quality only matters within it.
The lesson: Match language coupling capabilities to your context AND your version. C++23 with modern idioms is a different beast from C++98. Java 26 with virtual threads, records, and sealed classes is not Java 8. Don’t pick a language based on its worst version. Building life-critical systems? Use SPARK or Lean4. Building a 20-year system with changing requirements? Invest in Rust. Building mobile apps? Swift or Kotlin. Building a weekend project? JavaScript is fine. Maintaining legacy code? TypeScript adds coupling separation incrementally. Need shell automation? Fish or PowerShell beat Bash.
Stop chasing the perfect language. Pick one that fits your constraints, understand its coupling traps, and build with discipline.
The language wars are over. the analysis shows why: different contexts need different coupling trade-offs.
Now get back to building things.

title: The Great Language Smackdown: 65 Languages Through the Coupling Lens
text:
19 Learn More
The Independent Variation Principle is stated and proved in the published paper on the principle [11]:
The paper provides: - The statement of IVP: elements with the same change drivers belong together, elements with different change drivers belong apart - A graph-theoretic proof that grouping elements by their change-driver sets is the structure that minimizes change propagation cost - The counting argument on the element–change-driver incidence graph that makes the module boundaries a mathematical consequence rather than a design choice
The change-driver partition and the purity/completeness of the modules the coupling analysis presupposes are developed in Causal Cohesion [12], and the cohesion-as-correctness framework in On the Nature of Cohesion [13].

Which language’s coupling analysis surprised you? Did I miss critical coupling mechanisms? Share your experiences in the comments!

title: C# (13)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Interfaces + extension methods: Can add behavior without coupling to classes
✅ Generics with constraints: Better than Java (no erasure, value type generics)
✅ LINQ separates iteration from logic: Query syntax decouples data operations
⚠️ Inheritance still available: Can couple via class hierarchies
✅ Nullable reference types (C# 8+): Separates nullable from non-nullable
✅ File-scoped types (C# 11): file access modifier restricts visibility to a source file, tightening encapsulation

Object Construction:

✅ Object initializers decouple: new Person { Name = "Alice", Age = 30 }
✅ Records (C# 9+) are immutable: Value semantics prevent coupling
✅ Primary constructors (C# 12): Reduce construction boilerplate on class/struct
✅ Collection expressions (C# 12): [1, 2, 3] unified syntax decouples creation from collection type
⚠️ Constructors can have side effects: No enforcement of pure construction
✅ DI built into ASP.NET Core: Framework-level construction decoupling

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ .NET GC decouples memory: Generational GC (gen0, gen1, gen2, LOH)
✅ No manual memory management for managed code: Safe by default
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Server/workstation GC modes, background GC helps
✅ IDisposable pattern for resources: Deterministic cleanup via using statement
⚠️ Finalizers couple cleanup to GC: Non-deterministic timing
⚠️ Stack-allocated structs: Value types avoid GC but couple to stack lifetime
✅ Span reduces allocations: Stack-based memory without GC pressure

Error Handling:

❌ Unchecked exceptions: No throws clause, errors hidden
⚠️ Result types uncommon: Libraries exist (LanguageExt) but not idiomatic
⚠️ Nullable pattern helps: ?. operator reduces null coupling

Concurrency:

✅ Async/await excellent: Best async syntax in mainstream languages
✅ Task separates async: Clear distinction from sync code
✅ Lock type (C# 13): Dedicated System.Threading.Lock with pattern-based using scoping — decouples synchronization from object casting
❌ Can still use threads with shared state: Traditional coupling available
✅ Immutable collections available: System.Collections.Immutable, FrozenSet/FrozenDictionary (C# 12+) prevent concurrent coupling with zero overhead

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Null still exists alongside nullable types: Migration incomplete
❌ Static state couples: Singleton patterns common
❌ Properties can have side effects: obj.Prop might do anything
⚠️ .NET runtime allows reflection: Can break encapsulation

text: Analysis against Go 1.26 (February 2026). Generics have been stable since 1.18 (March 2022) — over 4 years of production use. Go 1.24 added generic type aliases; Go 1.26 adds further generic and runtime improvements.

title: Go (1.26)
text:
1 Coupling Analysis
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Implicit interfaces radical decoupling: No declaration of implementation, duck typing at compile time
✅ Composition over inheritance: No inheritance, only struct embedding
✅ Small interfaces: Convention is single-method interfaces (io.Reader, io.Writer)
✅ Generics (stable since 1.18): Type parameters eliminate interface{} casts — slices.Sort, maps.Clone, cmp.Or are type-safe (note: sync.Map remains a non-generic any-keyed type)
✅ Range-over-func (1.23): Custom iteration patterns via iter.Seq[T] decouple iteration protocol from data structure
⚠️ No higher-kinded types: Generics are first-order type parameters only
✅ min/max/clear builtins (1.21): Built-in operations eliminate unnecessary function coupling

Object Construction:

✅ Zero values make sense: Default initialization doesn’t couple to constructors
✅ Constructors are conventions: NewX() functions, not special syntax
⚠️ Can couple to package-level state: init() functions run at import

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory: Concurrent mark-sweep GC with sub-millisecond pause targets
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free
✅ Escape analysis optimizes: Stack allocation when possible, decouples from explicit allocation
✅ Profile-guided optimization (1.22+): Compiler uses runtime profiles to optimize, decoupling performance from manual tuning
⚠️ Defer couples cleanup to function exit: Not immediate, but predictable
✅ Simple memory model: No complex ownership rules

Error Handling:

✅ Explicit error returns: func foo() (Result, error) makes errors visible
❌ No error composition: Can’t map/flatMap errors natively
❌ if err != nil boilerplate: Error handling doesn’t compose
⚠️ Panic exists but rare: Explicit, but not in type system
⚠️ errors.Join (1.20): Can combine multiple errors, improving composition slightly

Concurrency:

✅ Goroutines separate concurrency: Lightweight, easy to spawn
✅ Channels separate communication: Message passing decouples
✅ Select decouples multiplexing: Wait on multiple channels independently
✅ Structured logging (slog, 1.21): Decouples logging concerns from application logic
⚠️ Can share memory: Mutexes allow traditional coupling, but discouraged

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Nil everywhere: nil pointers, nil interfaces couple code to nil checks (no sum types to replace nil)
❌ Global package state: Package-level variables couple to initialization order
❌ Error handling doesn’t compose: Repetitive if err != nil; generics enable Result types but not idiomatic
⚠️ Interfaces can be nil with non-nil value: (nil, *T) couples interface semantics

Core Coupling Score: 58/100 (Go 1.26 — mature generics, range-over-func, slog)

Verdict: Go’s implicit interfaces provide exceptionally low coupling by decoupling implementation from declaration without explicit implements clauses. Goroutines and channels separate concurrency from shared-memory synchronization. Generics, stable for over three years, eliminate interface{} casts. Range-over-func enables custom iteration without coupling to built-in loop constructs. Main strength: simplicity prevents complex coupling from emerging. Main weakness: nil is still everywhere, error handling does not compose, and the language has no sum types or pattern matching.

This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].

✅ Inline classes avoid boxing: Value classes reduce allocation overhead
⚠️ Lambda captures extend lifetimes: Closures hold references
⚠️ Java interop can leak: Calling Java code with memory-unsafe patterns

❌ Unchecked exceptions: Same as Java
✅ Result type in stdlib: Result<T> available but not widely used
✅ Null safety prevents NPE coupling: ?. and ?: operators

Concurrency:

✅ Coroutines excellent: Structured concurrency prevents leaks
✅ Suspending functions separate: suspend keyword makes async explicit
✅ Flow separates async streams: Cold streams decouple production from consumption

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Java interop allows nulls: Calling Java code bypasses null safety
⚠️ Companion objects can couple to static state: Like Java static methods
⚠️ Inheritance still available: Can create coupled hierarchies

title: Swift (6.2)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Protocols decouple interface from implementation: Similar to Rust traits
✅ Value types (structs) vs reference types (classes): Explicit separation
✅ Enums with associated values: Discriminated unions like Rust/F#
✅ Generics with constraints: <T: Equatable> decouples from concrete types
⚠️ Optional chaining: ?. syntax elegant but can hide nil propagation
❌ AnyObject/Any: Type erasure creates coupling escape hatch

Object Construction:

✅ Initializers separate from usage: init methods decouple construction
✅ Failable initializers: init? makes construction failure explicit
✅ Value semantics by default: Structs copy, preventing shared state coupling
⚠️ Classes allow inheritance: Can create coupling hierarchies
✅ Protocol-oriented programming: Composition over inheritance

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Automatic Reference Counting (ARC): Deterministic, no GC pauses
⚠️ Retain cycles possible: Weak/unowned references needed for graphs
✅ Value types: No reference counting for structs
✅ Predictable: Deallocation timing known
⚠️ Objective-C interop: Can introduce manual memory management

Error Handling:

✅ Typed throws (Swift 6): throws(MyError) makes error types explicit in signatures — a major coupling improvement over untyped throws
✅ Do-try-catch: Explicit error handling, checked at call site
✅ Result<T, E> available: For functional-style composable error handling
⚠️ Failable initializers: init? returns nil instead of throwing
⚠️ Force unwrap: ! bypasses safety, couples to runtime crash
✅ Guard statements: Early exit decouples validation from logic

Concurrency:

✅ Swift Concurrency (async/await): Built-in, structured concurrency
✅ Actors: Data race prevention via isolation
✅ Sendable protocol + strict concurrency checking (Swift 6, on by default): Compile-time thread safety with full enforcement
✅ Task-based: Decouples concurrent operations
⚠️ Grand Central Dispatch (GCD): Legacy API still available, manual

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Force unwrap (!): Bypasses type safety, couples to runtime crashes
❌ Implicitly unwrapped optionals: String! hides nil possibility
❌ Objective-C interop: Can bypass Swift safety guarantees
❌ Dynamic dispatch overhead: Protocol witness tables couple performance

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Value vs Reference: Structs vs Classes creates identity coupling decisions
ARC vs Manual: Retain cycles require weak/unowned discipline
Swift vs Objective-C: Interop couples to legacy patterns
Protocol Extensions: Default implementations can create hidden coupling

Core Coupling Score: 88/100 (Swift 6 — typed throws, strict concurrency checking)

title: The Objective Coupling Scoring Model: Full Mechanism Data for 65 Languages
text:
Companion to: The Great Language Smackdown: 65 Languages Through the Coupling Lens

The main article ranks 65 languages by language-imposed coupling. This companion publishes the complete per-language mechanism-presence data behind every score, so any reader can reproduce any number from first principles — no trust required.
The coupling analysis this model operationalizes — coupling as access to a shared resource, and the derivation of a modularisation directive from coupling — is developed in the published coupling papers [1], [2].
Analysis date: June 2026. All languages are assessed against the version shown.


The model is a capped-sum-per-dimension inventory:

A fixed mechanism inventory, each mechanism with a fixed weight.
For each language, every mechanism is marked present or absent (a factual determination).
Within each of the six Core dimensions (and eight Meta dimensions), the present weights are summed and clamped to at most −15.
Score = 100 − Σ(capped per-dimension contributions).

The cap equals the High weight (−15), so a dimension never costs more than one severe mechanism. This keeps scores bounded (minimum Core = 10), monotone (adding a mechanism never helps), and discriminative (no collapse to zero).


Because the model is a fixed-inventory capped-sum-per-dimension model, the bands follow directly from the mechanism weights:

90+: No dimension contains a severe (High) mechanism, and at most one dimension reaches even −8. Near the irreducible floor.
75–89: No dimension reaches −15; a small number of moderate (−8) mechanisms spread across dimensions.
60–74: At least one dimension caps at −15 (a severe mechanism), or several dimensions carry moderate mechanisms.
45–59: Two or three dimensions cap at −15, or one severe mechanism plus several moderate across other dimensions.
Below 45: Three or more dimensions cap at −15 — the language’s design trades separation of concerns for other goals (simplicity, flexibility, ubiquity, or direct hardware access).




The dimension sub-scores shown in the main article’s comparison matrices are the per-dimension contribution: 100 minus the capped sum of the present mechanisms in that dimension only. They are not independent scores — they are the building blocks of the composite, so a language’s Core score always equals 100 minus the sum of its six capped per-dimension contributions.

title: The Objective Coupling Scoring Model: Full Mechanism Data for 65 Languages
text:
The model is a capped-sum-per-dimension inventory:

A fixed mechanism inventory, each mechanism with a fixed weight.
For each language, every mechanism is marked present or absent (a factual determination).
Within each of the six Core dimensions (and eight Meta dimensions), the present weights are summed and clamped to at most −15.
Score = 100 − Σ(capped per-dimension contributions).

The cap equals the High weight (−15), so a dimension never costs more than one severe mechanism. This keeps scores bounded (minimum Core = 10), monotone (adding a mechanism never helps), and discriminative (no collapse to zero).


Because the model is a fixed-inventory capped-sum-per-dimension model, the bands follow directly from the mechanism weights:

90+: No dimension contains a severe (High) mechanism, and at most one dimension reaches even −8. Near the irreducible floor.
75–89: No dimension reaches −15; a small number of moderate (−8) mechanisms spread across dimensions.
60–74: At least one dimension caps at −15 (a severe mechanism), or several dimensions carry moderate mechanisms.
45–59: Two or three dimensions cap at −15, or one severe mechanism plus several moderate across other dimensions.
Below 45: Three or more dimensions cap at −15 — the language’s design trades separation of concerns for other goals (simplicity, flexibility, ubiquity, or direct hardware access).




The dimension sub-scores shown in the main article’s comparison matrices are the per-dimension contribution: 100 minus the capped sum of the present mechanisms in that dimension only. They are not independent scores — they are the building blocks of the composite, so a language’s Core score always equals 100 minus the sum of its six capped per-dimension contributions.

title: Bash (5.3)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

❌ Everything is strings: No type system whatsoever
❌ No abstractions: No functions (only shell functions), no interfaces
⚠️ Associative arrays: Bash 4+ has hashes, but limited
❌ No encapsulation: All variables global unless explicitly local
❌ No modules: Sourcing scripts pollutes namespace

Object Construction:

❌ No objects: Not an object-oriented language
❌ No constructors: Everything is imperative scripting
⚠️ Functions: Can simulate construction with functions
❌ No validation: Can’t enforce invariants

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Automatic: Shell manages memory for variables
✅ Process-based: Each script is a process, cleaned up on exit
⚠️ File descriptors: Must manually close, can leak
✅ No manual management: Can’t segfault (unless calling C programs)

Error Handling:

❌ Exit codes only: Return 0-255, no typed errors
❌ Ignores errors by default: Must use set -e to fail on errors
❌ No exceptions: Can’t catch/throw
⚠️ trap: Can handle signals, but limited
❌ Silent failures: Commands fail silently unless checked

Concurrency:

⚠️ Background jobs: & runs in background
❌ No coordination: No semaphores, mutexes in pure bash
⚠️ Pipes: Pipeline concurrency, but limited
❌ Race conditions: Easy to create, hard to avoid
⚠️ Process-based: Fork/exec model, heavyweight

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Global variables: All variables global unless local
❌ Environment variables: Implicit dependencies everywhere
❌ Word splitting: Unquoted variables couple to IFS
❌ Path dependencies: Couples to external commands availability
❌ Platform coupling: Bash version, coreutils differences

Core Coupling Score: 43/100

Verdict: Bash is a scripting language that trades nearly all separation-of-concerns enforcement for universal availability. Everything is a string, all variables are global by default, and errors are ignored unless explicitly checked. Its main strength is that it runs everywhere and excels at gluing Unix tools together. Its main weakness is pervasive coupling to the platform, the environment, and the availability of external commands. Use Bash for small automation, not for application development.

title: Fish (4.0)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 43/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 49/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Fish is a modern rethink of shell design. It uses functions instead of aliases, which provides better decoupling between invocation name and behavior. No variable quoting is needed because arrays are first-class citizens. Configuration is stored in separate files, decoupling shell setup from scripting logic. Autosuggestions help users discover commands without needing to memorize exact syntax. While values are still string-based, Fish provides better array and list handling than Bash. Not being POSIX-compatible couples script portability to Fish-specific syntax.
Platform & Ecosystem: Fish excels at interactive use thanks to a polished out-of-box experience. It provides a web-based configuration GUI, built-in syntax highlighting, and fast autocompletions. The ecosystem is small but growing. Its lack of POSIX compatibility creates portability issues for scripts written in Fish. Performance is good because Fish is implemented in C++. The learning curve is gentle; Fish is cleaner and more consistent than Bash or Zsh.

title: Zsh (5.9)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Core Coupling Score: 43/100 | Platform & Ecosystem Score: 68/100
Core Coupling Analysis: Zsh is similar to Bash but improves on several fronts. Arrays are indexed starting from 1, as in Lua. Zsh provides more expressive globbing than Bash, which decouples pattern matching from the limitations of standard wildcards. Associative arrays are built into the language. However, everything remains a string at heart, providing no type safety. Functions are more capable than Bash functions but remain global by default. Prompt theme systems like oh-my-zsh separate shell appearance configuration from script logic. Parameter expansion is more powerful than in Bash but also more complex, coupling effective use to deep expertise.
Platform & Ecosystem: Zsh excels at interactive use, especially with frameworks like oh-my-zsh. Its completion system is better than Bash’s. Zsh is now the default shell on macOS, having replaced Bash. A rich plugin ecosystem through frameworks like oh-my-zsh improves user ergonomics. Zsh is faster than Bash for some operations and provides a POSIX compatibility mode. The learning curve is moderate since Bash knowledge transfers. However, Zsh is not as ubiquitous as Bash, making scripts written in Zsh less portable.

title: C (C23)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Structs separate data: Pure data, no methods
✅ Function pointers enable polymorphism: Can pass behavior as data
❌ No encapsulation: Everything is public
❌ No generics: Void pointers couple to type casting
✅ No inheritance: Can’t create coupled hierarchies

Object Construction:

✅ Explicit memory management: Allocation separate from initialization
✅ Designated initializers: Can initialize specific fields
❌ No constructors: Manual initialization couples to usage
❌ Global state common: Static variables couple modules

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Manual control enables precise memory strategy: Can separate memory management from logic
✅ Explicit allocation/deallocation: malloc/free make lifetime visible
❌ No safety: use-after-free, double-free, memory leaks all possible
❌ No RAII: Must manually track and free resources
✅ Predictable: No GC pauses, deterministic performance
❌ Pointer arithmetic couples to memory layout: Buffer overruns couple to hardware
✅ Custom allocators: Can decouple allocation strategy (arena, pool, etc.)
❌ Undefined behavior on errors: Memory safety violations are UB

Error Handling:

✅ Explicit error codes: Return values make errors visible
❌ No enforcement: Can ignore return values
❌ errno couples: Global error state couples functions
❌ NULL everywhere: Pointer errors couple all code

Concurrency:

❌ pthreads manual: All synchronization explicit
❌ Shared mutable state default: No protection
❌ Data races are undefined behavior: No prevention
⚠️ Explicit is predictable: At least coupling is visible

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Pointers couple to memory layout: No abstraction over memory
❌ Header files couple: Includes create compilation dependencies
❌ Macros couple: Preprocessor doesn’t respect scope
❌ No namespaces: Global namespace pollution
❌ Undefined behavior: Buffer overruns, null derefs

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Power vs. Safety: Complete control couples to complete responsibility for safety
Simplicity vs. Safety: No abstractions means manual discipline required to control coupling
Performance vs. Correctness: Optimization couples to unsafe patterns (buffer tricks, pointer arithmetic)
Portability vs. Platform Access: Platform-specific code couples to hardware/OS
Manual Memory Management: Must couple resource acquisition to every usage site
Undefined Behavior Everywhere: Memory errors couple entire program to runtime environment
Header Dependencies: Changes to one header couple to all files that include it (transitively)

With discipline, developers can separate concerns through function pointers, explicit error codes, and manual memory management. title: Haskell (GHC 9.12)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Pure functions separate side effects from pure logic: The type system (IO monad) keeps effects isolated, preventing hidden coupling to global state
✅ Type classes enable polymorphism without inheritance coupling: Abstraction through type classes (Functor, Monad, etc.) decouples interface from implementation
✅ Parametric polymorphism prevents coupling to concrete types: map :: (a -> b) -> [a] -> [b] works for any types without knowing their internals
⚠️ Monad transformers can create coupling: Stacking monads (ReaderT, StateT, ExceptT) creates order-dependent coupling

Object Construction:

✅ Data constructors separate shape from creation logic: ADTs (Algebraic Data Types) decouple data structure from construction
✅ Smart constructors enable validation without coupling: Can wrap raw constructors to add invariants
✅ No shared mutable state: Construction doesn’t couple to global state

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ Garbage collection decouples memory from logic: Don’t think about deallocation
✅ Immutability simplifies GC: No cyclic references from mutable structures
⚠️ GC pauses couple to runtime: Non-deterministic pauses affect real-time requirements
⚠️ Space leaks from lazy evaluation: Thunks accumulate, coupling evaluation strategy to memory usage
✅ No manual memory management: Can’t have use-after-free or double-free bugs

Error Handling:

✅ Either/Maybe separate success from failure: Either Error Result makes error path explicit and separate from success path
✅ Exceptions are typed: IO exceptions are contained in IO monad, preventing hidden coupling
⚠️ Partial functions (head, tail) can couple: Runtime errors bypass type system unless avoided

Concurrency:

✅ STM (Software Transactional Memory) decouples concurrency from logic: Composable transactions separate concurrent coordination from business logic
✅ Immutability prevents temporal coupling: No shared mutable state means concurrent operations don’t interfere
✅ Async/threading is explicit in types: Concurrency concerns are separate via type signatures

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ IO monad couples all effects: Can’t separate file IO from network IO from randomness at type level (without effect systems)
❌ Lazy evaluation couples computation order to memory management: Space leaks occur when evaluation strategy couples to resource usage
❌ Global type class instances couple: Orphan instances create action-at-a-distance coupling

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Performance vs. Abstraction: Lazy evaluation optimizes for composability but couples performance to evaluation strategy
Purity vs. Practicality: IO monad is all-or-nothing—can’t separate different IO types without mtl/effect systems
Type Class Coherence vs. Modularity: Only one instance per type globally couples modules that define instances
Laziness vs. Predictability: Space/time behavior depends on evaluation order, creating hidden coupling
Monad Transformer Order: ReaderT (StateT (ExceptT ...)) ≠ StateT (ReaderT (ExceptT ...)), order matters

title: Scala (3.8 / 3.3 LTS)
text:
This assessment follows the coupling analysis of the Independent Variation Principle [1]; the language is assessed against its official reference [2].
Type System & Abstraction:

✅ Traits enable composition: Multiple trait inheritance without diamond problem
✅ Implicit parameters decouple: Can pass context without threading parameters
✅ Higher-kinded types: Generic over type constructors (Map, List, Option)
⚠️ Implicits can create hidden coupling: Action-at-a-distance when implicit resolution isn’t obvious

Object Construction:

✅ Case classes separate data from construction: Immutable, auto-generated constructors
✅ Apply methods decouple construction syntax: Person("Alice", 30) instead of new Person(...)
⚠️ Can use Java-style mutable constructors: Interop allows coupled patterns

Memory Management & Deallocation:

✅ JVM GC decouples memory: Generational GC handles deallocation
✅ Immutable collections reduce GC pressure: Structural sharing, persistent data structures
⚠️ GC pauses affect latency: Stop-the-world pauses, though modern JVM GC improves (ZGC, Shenandoah)
⚠️ Object allocation overhead: Boxing/unboxing couples primitives to heap allocation
⚠️ Closure captures can extend lifetimes: Function closures hold references, preventing collection

Error Handling:

✅ Try/Either/Option separate concerns: Multiple error handling approaches
✅ For-comprehensions make error composition clear: for { a <- tryA; b <- tryB } yield f(a, b)
❌ Exceptions still common: Scala culture uses exceptions more than Haskell-style Result

Concurrency:

✅ Futures decouple async: Future[T] separates async from sync
✅ Akka actors separate concurrent operations: Message passing prevents shared state
✅ Immutable collections by default: Prevents concurrent modification coupling
⚠️ Can use Java threads: Interop allows traditional coupling

Language-imposed coupling costs:

❌ Complexity allows many ways to couple: Language flexibility means discipline required
❌ Slow compilation couples dev workflow: Build time affects iteration speed
❌ Implicits can hide dependencies: Resolution order matters, creates coupling

Trade-offs (not coupling):

Expressiveness vs. Simplicity: Multiple ways to solve problems couples team to arbitrary choices
Implicits as Magic: Implicit resolution hides dependencies, creating action-at-a-distance coupling
Compile Time vs. Development Speed: Type-level programming couples fast iteration to long compile times
OOP + FP Hybrid: Can use both paradigms, but mixing couples code to dual mental models
Library Fragmentation: Cats vs. Scalaz vs. ZIO couples projects to ecosystem factions

text:
Software research and analysis. Software design is the broad concern; architecture is a part of design, but not all design is architecture.
This section is organized under the design concern:

Design — the design concern, containing architecture, languages, and principles.

The change-management account of module structure that informs the software analysis is published in the paper on the Independent Variation Principle [1].
